M04-front-P002.title: The gift of Dhamma and aspiration

paragraphs.M04-front-P002-S01:
Sabbadānaṃ dhammadānaṃ jināti.
Sabbarasaṃ dhammaraso jināti.
Sabbaratiṃ dhammarati jināti.
Taṇhakkhayo sabbadukkhaṃ jināti.
paragraphs.M04-front-P002-S02:
The gift of Dhamma surpasses every gift.
The taste of Dhamma surpasses every taste.
Delight in Dhamma surpasses every delight.
The destruction of craving overcomes all suffering.
paragraphs.M04-front-P002-S03: Ciraṃ tiṭṭhatu saddhammo, dhamme hontu sagāravā.
paragraphs.M04-front-P002-S04:
May the Buddha’s dispensation endure for a long time.
May all honour the three kinds of true Dhamma.

M04-body-P001.title: What to know about consciousness — A hundred thousand koṭis

paragraphs.M04-body-P001-S02: Meditation on Mentality. Part 1. What to know about consciousness.
paragraphs.M04-body-P001-S03:
Ekaccharakkhaṇe koṭisatasahassasaṅkhyā uppajjitvā nirujjhanti. (Saṃyutta Nikāya Commentary, vol. 2, p. 295.)
In a finger snap, a hundred thousand koṭis arise and cease.
paragraphs.M04-body-P001-S04: In the time it takes to blink, for lightning to flash, or to snap the fingers, mental phenomena arise and cease more than a hundred thousand koṭis of times. Citing such statements in the texts, people repeatedly challenge practitioners with that number: “How can one discern mental phenomena arising and ceasing more than a hundred thousand koṭis of times in the blink of an eye, a flash of lightning, or a snap of the fingers?” Thus a meditation subject that once flourished receives little favour in today’s insight circles, as though it lay quietly hidden in a corner of the dispensation. We have now reached the section on apprehending and discerning those mental phenomena. May all good friends of pure heart apply themselves diligently to developing this meditation subject.

M04-body-P002.title: Three ways to apprehend mental phenomena

paragraphs.M04-body-P002-S01:
Tividho hi arūpakammaṭṭhāne abhiniveso phassavasena vedanāvasena cittavasenāti. (Dīgha Nikāya Commentary, vol. 2, p. 314; Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, vol. 1, p. 280; Abhidhamma Commentary, vol. 2, p. 252.)
There are three ways of entering meditation on mentality, by way of contact, feeling, or consciousness.
paragraphs.M04-body-P002-S02:
There are three ways to begin meditation on mentality, that is, to begin distinguishing mental phenomena with wisdom:
1. Begin apprehending them from contact, for those to whom contact is prominent.
2. Begin from feeling, for those to whom feeling is prominent.
3. Begin from consciousness, for those to whom consciousness is prominent.
paragraphs.M04-body-P002-S03: If you are a practitioner whose vehicle is pure insight (suddhavipassanāyānika), take the following guideline to heart and follow it when beginning meditation on mentality.
paragraphs.M04-body-P002-S04: Yasmā ca evaṃ suvisuddharūpapariggahasseva tassa arūpadhammā tīhākārehi pākaṭā honti. Tasmā suvisuddharūpapariggaheneva arūpapariggahāya yogo kātabbo, na itarena. Sace hi ekasmiṃ vā rūpadhamme upaṭṭhite dvīsu vā rūpaṃ pahāya arūpapariggahaṃ ārabhati kammaṭṭhānato parihāyati, pathavīkasiṇabhāvanāya vuttappakārā pabbateyyā gāvī viya. Suvisuddharūpapariggahassa pana arūpapariggahāya yogaṃ karoto kammaṭṭhānaṃ vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ pāpuṇāti. (Visuddhimagga, vol. 2, p. 227.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P002-S05: Mental phenomena become clear in those three ways when one’s apprehension of materiality is thoroughly purified. Therefore, undertake the apprehension of mentality once the apprehension of materiality is thoroughly purified. If one or two material phenomena have become evident and one abandons materiality to begin apprehending mentality, one falls away from the meditation subject, like the mountain cow described in the development of the earth kasiṇa. When one whose apprehension of materiality is thoroughly purified works at apprehending mentality, the meditation subject grows, develops and comes to fullness.
paragraphs.M04-body-P002-S06: A lower jhāna that has been well developed and brought to mastery serves as the basis and principal condition for a higher jhāna. Mere attainment does not suffice. So it is with the apprehension of materiality … (Mahāṭīkā, vol. 2, p. 357. The quotation continues on Burmese page 3.)

M04-body-P003.title: Apprehending materiality as the basis for discerning mentality

paragraphs.M04-body-P003-S01: … The apprehension of materiality, once purified and cleared of impediments, serves as the basis and principal condition for apprehending mentality. Thus, when even a portion of the apprehension of materiality and mentality has yet to develop, there is no growth. This is all the clearer for someone in whom many portions remain undeveloped. Hence the text says “sace hi”, “for if”, and so on. (Mahāṭīkā, vol. 2, p. 357.) [The Latin transcription of the quotation continued from page 2 is pending, particularly the phrase just before eva arūpapariggahassa.]
paragraphs.M04-body-P003-S02: If you take pure insight as your vehicle, first become one whose apprehension of materiality is thoroughly purified (suvisuddharūpapariggaha), that is, one who has clearly distinguished and apprehended material phenomena with wisdom. In the continuum of a being with all five aggregates, eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue- and body-sensitivity are the material bases on which the groups of mental phenomena called eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue- and body-consciousness arise in the regular course of events. The groups of mental phenomena called mind element and mind-consciousness element arise dependent on the heart-base, with the life-continuum, the clear mind-door, supporting the process.
paragraphs.M04-body-P003-S03: Thus, if you cannot yet apprehend and discern the respective material bases on which those mental phenomena arise, and the life-continuum, the clear mind-door, you are still far from apprehending and distinguishing mental phenomena with wisdom to the level of ultimate reality and breaking up mental compactness.
paragraphs.M04-body-P003-S04: Why? Only in the knowledge of a meditator who has thoroughly purified the apprehension of materiality do mental phenomena become evident by one or by all three of the ways of apprehending and discerning mentality described above. Therefore, thoroughly purify the apprehension of materiality …

paragraphs.M04-body-P004-S01: … and only when a meditator has apprehended materiality should they make an effort to apprehend mental phenomena. One who has yet to apprehend material phenomena thoroughly and clearly should refrain from attempting to apprehend mentality. If, when just one or two material phenomena have become evident to wisdom, one stops developing meditation on materiality and abandons apprehending materiality to undertake apprehension of mentality, one may regress and lose the meditation subject. (Visuddhimagga, vol. 2, p. 227, para. 671.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P004-S02: The comparison is with a lower jhāna developed well enough to attain the five masteries. Only such a jhāna can serve as the foundation and closest cause for a higher jhāna. Mere attainment of a lower jhāna cannot serve as the foundation and proximate condition for a higher one. Likewise, only knowledge that apprehends materiality (rūpapariggahañāṇa) thoroughly and clearly, free from confusion and blemish, can be the foundation and closest cause for knowledge that apprehends mentality (arūpapariggahañāṇa). Until the former is purified, it cannot serve as that foundation and closest cause. Thus even if only a portion of material and mental phenomena fails to appear clearly to the meditator’s wisdom, that knowledge of apprehending materiality is still called unpurified. If many…

M04-body-P005.title: The simile of the mountain cow

paragraphs.M04-body-P005-S01: … material and mental phenomena fail to appear clearly and are not seen by wisdom, what more need be said? The commentator spoke as above to make this meaning clear. (Mahāṭīkā, vol. 2, p. 357.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P005-S02: In the Aṅguttara Nikāya (vol. 3, p. 216), the Buddha taught the Discourse on the Simile of the Cow (Gāvī-upamā Sutta). He spoke of a foolish, clumsy cow unskilled in grazing on rugged mountains. Looking out from a spot on the mountaintop, it saw a large lake of clear, cool water with lush grass and foliage around it. Intending to eat the tender grass and leaves and drink the clear, cool water, it descended. Before planting its front foot firmly, it lifted its hind foot. It tumbled down the mountain. It could neither eat the grass and leaves it had hoped for nor drink the water, and could not climb back to its former place.
paragraphs.M04-body-P005-S03: Likewise, the Buddha taught that if a meditating bhikkhu attempts a higher jhāna before training to attain the five masteries over a lower jhāna, he may fail to reach the higher jhāna and fall away from the lower one already attained. (For details, see the Discourse on the Simile of the Cow.)

M04-body-P006.title: Discerning mentality with tranquillity as the vehicle

paragraphs.M04-body-P006-S01: Using the same simile, the commentator warns that if one tries to apprehend the subject of mentality before thoroughly purifying one's apprehension of materiality, one may regress and lose the meditation subject. The hoped-for progress in mentality may fail to come, and the progress already made in materiality may be lost.
paragraphs.M04-body-P006-S02: If you take tranquillity as your vehicle (samathayānika), the strength of jhāna concentration enables you to begin by apprehending the mental phenomena of jhāna, led by factors such as applied thought, sustained thought, joy, pleasure and one-pointedness. After apprehending them, continue with the heart-base on which they arise and the accompanying great elements and derived materiality. This is the instruction of the Visuddhimagga (vol. 2, p. 222). Then, when continuing to apprehend the five aggregates subject to clinging, called formations that have ripened (pakkasaṅkhāra), you must also apprehend sense-sphere mental phenomena. By that stage it is especially necessary to have apprehended the respective material bases. Therefore, when apprehending sense-sphere mental phenomena, the tranquillity practitioner should also take the guideline to heart and follow it, just as the pure-insight practitioner should.
paragraphs.M04-body-P006-S03: If, without developing either of the two kinds of concentration, access or absorption, and without following the guideline above, you begin meditation on mentality…

paragraphs.M04-body-P007-S01: … that is, attempt the meditation work of apprehending and discerning mental phenomena, you too might become one of those who use the number of a hundred thousand koṭis to challenge the Buddha’s teaching on mental phenomena.
paragraphs.M04-body-P007-S02:
Tassevaṃ pariggahitarūpassa dvāravasena arūpadhammā pākaṭā honti. (Visuddhimagga, vol. 2, p. 223.)
For one who has thus apprehended materiality, mental phenomena become evident by way of the doors.
paragraphs.M04-body-P007-S03:
Kāmaṃ vatthuvasenāpi arūpadhammā pākaṭā honti, dvāravasena pana pariggaho anākuloti katvā vuttaṃ “dvāravasena arūpadhammā pākaṭā hontī”ti. (Mahāṭīkā, vol. 2, pp. 352–353.)
Mental phenomena are also evident by way of their bases. Since apprehension by way of the doors is free of confusion, the text says, “mental phenomena become evident by way of the doors.”
paragraphs.M04-body-P007-S04: In apprehending mental phenomena one may proceed by way of the material bases or by way of the doors classed as sense bases, as in the eye-door and ear-door processes. Of the two methods, the commentator explains that mental phenomena become evident by way of the doors classed as sense bases to a meditator who has thoroughly purified the apprehension of materiality. There is a reason for that instruction.
paragraphs.M04-body-P007-S05:
1. Mental phenomena arising dependent on the eye-base.
2. Mental phenomena arising dependent on the ear-base.
3. Mental phenomena arising dependent on the nose-base.

M04-body-P008.title: Further explanation of bases and doors

paragraphs.M04-body-P008-S01:
4. Mental phenomena arising dependent on the tongue-base.
5. Mental phenomena arising dependent on the body-base.
6. Mental phenomena arising dependent on the heart-base.
paragraphs.M04-body-P008-S02: When mental phenomena are apprehended in this way by their supporting bases, there is overlap. By door, however, there are six groups: the mental phenomena of eye-door, ear-door, nose-door, tongue-door, body-door and mind-door processes.
paragraphs.M04-body-P008-S03: Apprehending these groups by the doors classed as sense bases is free of confusion (anākula). The commentator therefore instructs one to apprehend mental phenomena by such doors, for example the group of mental phenomena in an eye-door process. (Visuddhimagga, vol. 2, p. 223; Mahāṭīkā, vol. 2, pp. 352–353.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P008-S04:
1. The mental group of eye-consciousness arises dependent on the eye-base.
2. The mental group of ear-consciousness arises dependent on the ear-base.
3. The mental group of nose-consciousness arises dependent on the nose-base.
4. The mental group of tongue-consciousness arises dependent on the tongue-base…

paragraphs.M04-body-P009-S01:
… 5. The mental group of body-consciousness arises dependent on the body-base.
6. The mental groups called mind element and mind-consciousness element arise dependent on the heart-base.
paragraphs.M04-body-P009-S02: The respective mental groups dependent on the eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue- and body-bases do not overlap. The groups dependent on the heart-base, however, can take any of the six objects as appropriate, so there is overlap. For a clearer understanding, see the tables in the section on meditation on mentality. Consider also the classification by object:
paragraphs.M04-body-P009-S03:
1. Visible form: the mental phenomena in eye-door and mind-door processes that take visible form as object.
2. Sound: the mental phenomena in ear-door and mind-door processes that take sound as object.
3. Odour: the mental phenomena in nose-door and mind-door processes that take odour as object.
4. Taste: the mental phenomena in tongue-door and mind-door processes that take taste as object.
5. Tangible object: the mental phenomena in body-door and mind-door processes that take a tangible object.
6. Mind-object: the mental phenomena in mind-door processes that take a mind-object.
paragraphs.M04-body-P009-S04: Thus apprehending mental phenomena by the doors classed as sense bases is free of confusion. That is why the commentator instructs one to apprehend mental phenomena by those doors…

M04-body-P010.title: Two practical rules and the scope of mundane mentality

paragraphs.M04-body-P010-S01: … If you wish to apprehend mental phenomena, especially if you take pure insight as your vehicle, take these two rules to heart: (1) First apprehend material phenomena. (2) Apprehend mental phenomena by the doors classed as sense bases. Apply yourself so that you do not become one who uses the number of a hundred thousand koṭis to challenge the Buddha’s teaching on mental phenomena.
paragraphs.M04-body-P010-S02:
Āyatanadvāravasenāti āyatanasaṅkhātadvāravasena. Kammadvāranivattanatthaṃ āyatanaggahaṇaṃ. (Mahāṭīkā, vol. 2, p. 410.)
“By the doors classed as sense bases” means by doors called sense bases. “Sense bases” is specified to exclude the doors of action.
paragraphs.M04-body-P010-S03: In the dispensation, “door” is used in two senses. The three doors of body, speech and mind are called doors of action (kammadvāra). The six doors of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind are called doors classed as sense bases (āyatanadvāra). Apprehend mental phenomena by these doors and in the order of consciousnesses in the process, using wisdom to break up the compactness that makes mentality appear as a solid mass, so that wisdom reaches ultimate reality. (The four kinds of mental compactness will be presented later.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P010-S04:
Mundane mental phenomena only. Lokuttaracittāni pana neva suddhavipassakassa, na samathayānikassa pariggahaṃ gacchanti anadhigatattā. (Visuddhimagga, vol. 2, p. 223.)
Supramundane consciousnesses fall within the apprehension of neither the pure-insight practitioner nor the practitioner with tranquillity as vehicle at this stage, since they have yet to attain them.
paragraphs.M04-body-P010-S05: In setting out the mental phenomena that are objects of insight knowledge, the Visuddhimagga says…

M04-body-P011.title: Mundane consciousnesses within the scope of discernment

paragraphs.M04-body-P011-S01:
Ekāsīti lokiyacittāni. (Visuddhimagga, vol. 2, p. 223.)
“Eighty-one mundane consciousnesses.” This indicates groups of mundane mental phenomena consisting of consciousness and mental factors. Since supramundane consciousness has yet to be attained, neither pure-insight practitioners nor those with tranquillity as vehicle can apprehend it. On this point the author of the Great Subcommentary explains as follows.
paragraphs.M04-body-P011-S02:
Sabbasaṅgāhikavasena “ekāsīti lokiyacittānī”ti vuttaṃ, lābhino eva pana mahaggatacittāni supākaṭāni honti. (Mahāṭīkā, vol. 2, p. 353.)
“Eighty-one mundane consciousnesses” is a comprehensive enumeration. Exalted consciousnesses become quite evident only to those who have attained them.
paragraphs.M04-body-P011-S03: The statement that all eighty-one mundane consciousnesses and their associated phenomena are objects of insight knowledge is made by way of a comprehensive count of the consciousnesses that can be its objects. Exalted consciousnesses can become evident only to the knowledge of meditators who have attained jhāna. (Mahāṭīkā, vol. 2, p. 353.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P011-S04: Only meditators who have attained jhāna can discern exalted consciousnesses. Thus, when apprehending mental phenomena, those who have attained jhāna should also apprehend and discern the mental phenomena of the jhāna they have attained. Pure-insight practitioners who have not attained jhāna may leave that discernment aside. Likewise, functional impulsions can arise only in the continuum of arahants. Thus when apprehending materiality and mentality or developing insight, worldlings and trainees may…

M04-body-P012.title: What to know before discerning mentality

paragraphs.M04-body-P012-S02: Consciousness cannot arise on its own without mental factors. Mental factors likewise cannot arise on their own without consciousness. In each consciousness moment they arise together in groups. Therefore know beforehand the consciousnesses and mental factors you will apprehend and discern at the stage of insight.
paragraphs.M04-body-P012-S03: Broadly, consciousness is of two kinds: consciousness in a cognitive process and consciousness outside a process (vīthimutta). The latter has three kinds: rebirth-linking, life-continuum and death consciousness. The first consciousness to arise in a life is rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta), since it links the previous life and the new life, and the aggregates of the two lives. The final consciousness to arise in a life is death consciousness (cuticitta), the life-continuum consciousness at departure from the present life. Between rebirth-linking and death, whenever process consciousnesses are absent, resultant consciousness of the same kind as rebirth-linking arises as a factor sustaining the continuity of the resultant aggregates and the stream of consciousness throughout that life, for as long as the kamma has power. It is called life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅgacitta). It stops when process consciousnesses arise and arises repeatedly again when they cease. This occurs throughout a life. The mental phenomena accompanying life-continuum consciousness generally become accessible after one has apprehended process consciousnesses…

M04-body-P013.title: The six bases and six doors

paragraphs.M04-body-P013-S01: … especially when they reach knowledge of apprehending conditions (paccayapariggahañāṇa). For this reason, a meditator wishing to apprehend mental phenomena should begin with the mental groups in the succession of process consciousnesses. Before apprehending mental phenomena in cognitive processes, one should know the following sets of six.
paragraphs.M04-body-P013-S02:
Six bases (vatthu), the material supports on which mental phenomena arise:
1. The eye-base (cakkhuvatthu) is eye-sensitivity (cakkhupasāda), the transparent materiality of the eye.
2. The ear-base (sotavatthu) is ear-sensitivity (sotapasāda), the transparent materiality of the ear.
3. The nose-base (ghānavatthu) is nose-sensitivity (ghānapasāda), the transparent materiality of the nose.
4. The tongue-base (jivhāvatthu) is tongue-sensitivity (jivhāpasāda), the transparent materiality of the tongue.
5. The body-base (kāyavatthu) is body-sensitivity (kāyapasāda), the transparent materiality of the body.
6. The heart-base (hadayavatthu) is heart materiality (hadayarūpa), the material support for the mind element and mind-consciousness element.
paragraphs.M04-body-P013-S03:
Six doors (dvāra):
1. The eye-door (cakkhudvāra) is eye-sensitivity.
2. The ear-door (sotadvāra) is ear-sensitivity.
3. The nose-door (ghānadvāra) is nose-sensitivity.
4. The tongue-door (jivhādvāra) is tongue-sensitivity.
5. The body-door (kāyadvāra) is body-sensitivity.
6. The mind-door (manodvāra) is the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), the clear mind.
paragraphs.M04-body-P013-S04: An opening fitted to a house for people to enter and leave, which can be opened and closed, is literally a door. People cannot enter a house without a door. Just as a doorway is where people enter…

M04-body-P014.title: Six objects and six kinds of mind-object

paragraphs.M04-body-P014-S01: … likewise, without eye-sensitivity and the other sensitivities, the consciousnesses of the eye-door process and the corresponding processes cannot arise. Eye-sensitivity and the other sensitivities within the body serve, as it were, as entrances for consciousnesses in their respective processes. By analogy with the ordinary doors fitted to a house, eye-sensitivity and the other sensitivities are called the eye-door and the corresponding doors.
paragraphs.M04-body-P014-S02:
Six objects:
1. Visible object (rūpārammaṇa) is colour (vaṇṇa).
2. Sound object (saddārammaṇa) is sound.
3. Odour object (gandhārammaṇa) is odour.
4. Taste object (rasārammaṇa) is taste.
5. Tangible object (phoṭṭhabbārammaṇa) is what can be touched: earth, fire and wind.
6. Mind-object (dhammārammaṇa) comprises phenomena that serve as objects of mind.
paragraphs.M04-body-P014-S03:
Six kinds of mind-object:
1. Sensitive materiality (pasādarūpa): the five kinds of transparent materiality.
2. Subtle materiality (sukhumarūpa): sixteen kinds of subtle materiality.
3. Consciousness (citta): the six consciousness elements.
4. Mental factors (cetasika): the fifty-two phenomena associated with consciousness.
5. Nibbāna: the unconditioned, the element of peace.
6. Concepts (paññatti): various concepts, such as kasiṇas, names and shapes.
paragraphs.M04-body-P014-S04: Note. The twelve kinds of materiality comprising the five sensitivities and the seven kinds of objective materiality…

M04-body-P015.title: The meaning of object and the first consciousness elements

paragraphs.M04-body-P015-S01: … readily become evident and are easily seen in the meditator’s knowledge when discerning. Being coarse, they are called gross materiality (oḷārikarūpa). Of the twenty-eight kinds of materiality, the sixteen remaining apart from the twelve gross kinds do not readily become evident to the knowledge of the meditator. Being subtle, they are called subtle materiality (sukhumarūpa).
paragraphs.M04-body-P015-S02: Ārammaṇa and ālambana are synonymous terms for an object. Ārammaṇa means a place of delight. Just as a garden with flowers is a place of delight for people, the six objects, beginning with visible form, are places of delight for consciousness and mental factors. Thus they are called ārammaṇa. Ālambana means something to hold on to. Just as a person who is weak needs to hold on to a stick, a rope or some other support to get up or sit down, consciousness and mental factors can arise only by relying on and taking hold of an object. So the six objects are also called ālambana, what consciousness and mental factors rely on and take hold of.
paragraphs.M04-body-P015-S03:
Six consciousness elements:
1. Eye-consciousness arises dependent on eye-sensitivity and knows only visible form.
2. Ear-consciousness arises dependent on ear-sensitivity and knows only sound.
3. Nose-consciousness arises dependent on nose-sensitivity and knows only odour…

M04-body-P016.title: The remaining consciousness elements and the six cognitive processes

paragraphs.M04-body-P016-S01:
4. Tongue-consciousness arises dependent on tongue-sensitivity and knows only taste.
5. Body-consciousness arises dependent on body-sensitivity and knows only a tangible object.
6. Mind-consciousness arises dependent on the heart-base, with the life-continuum, the clear mind-door, supporting the process, and knows the six objects as appropriate.
paragraphs.M04-body-P016-S02: Apart from the five pairs of consciousnesses under items 1–5, all consciousnesses arising dependent on the heart-base are termed mind-consciousness in the sense used here. They are consciousnesses that know objects in various ways. Except for the three kinds of consciousness outside a process, the remaining mind-consciousnesses, as well as the five kinds of sense consciousness above, arise in the fixed order of consciousness called a cognitive process (vīthi). In brief, there are six processes.
paragraphs.M04-body-P016-S03:
The six processes by door:
1. Eye-door process (cakkhudvāravīthi): the succession of consciousnesses arising at the eye-door.
2. Ear-door process (sotadvāravīthi): the succession arising at the ear-door.
3. Nose-door process (ghānadvāravīthi): the succession arising at the nose-door.
4. Tongue-door process (jivhādvāravīthi): the succession arising at the tongue-door.
5. Body-door process (kāyadvāravīthi): the succession arising at the body-door.
6. Mind-door process (manodvāravīthi): the succession arising at the mind-door.
These are reckoned by door. They may also be reckoned…

M04-body-P017.title: Naming processes by consciousness and the order of their moments

paragraphs.M04-body-P017-S01:
1. Eye-consciousness process (cakkhuviññāṇavīthi): the process named for eye-consciousness.
2. Ear-consciousness process (sotaviññāṇavīthi): the process named for ear-consciousness.
3. Nose-consciousness process (ghānaviññāṇavīthi): the process named for nose-consciousness.
4. Tongue-consciousness process (jivhāviññāṇavīthi): the process named for tongue-consciousness.
5. Body-consciousness process (kāyaviññāṇavīthi): the process named for body-consciousness.
6. Mind-consciousness process (manoviññāṇavīthi): the process named for mind-consciousness.
paragraphs.M04-body-P017-S02: Thus there are also six processes reckoned by consciousness. When visible form appears at the eye-door, the succession of consciousnesses taking it as object is called the eye-door process. When sound appears at the ear-door, the succession taking that sound as object is called the ear-door process. Pe. When a mind-object appears at the mind-door, or when any of the six objects appears there as appropriate, the succession taking that object is called the mind-door process. The processes are also named for their consciousnesses, as follows.
paragraphs.M04-body-P017-S03:
1. Eye-door process: five-door adverting, eye-consciousness, receiving, investigating, determining, seven impulsion moments and two registration moments.
2. Ear-door process: five-door adverting, ear-consciousness, receiving, investigating, determining, seven impulsion moments and two registration moments.
3. Nose-door process: five-door adverting, nose-consciousness, receiving, investigating, determining, seven impulsion moments and two registration moments.

M04-body-P018.title: Cognitive processes and the presentation of objects

paragraphs.M04-body-P018-S01:
4. Tongue-door process: five-door adverting, tongue-consciousness, receiving, investigating, determining, seven impulsion moments and two registration moments.
5. Body-door process: five-door adverting, body-consciousness, receiving, investigating, determining, seven impulsion moments and two registration moments.
6. Mind-door process: mind-door adverting, seven impulsion moments and two registration moments.
paragraphs.M04-body-P018-S02: The consciousnesses that distinguish these processes are those such as eye- and ear-consciousness. Five-door adverting, receiving and the like do not distinguish them. The process is therefore called the eye-consciousness process and so on, after its distinctive consciousness. The mind-door process has no such distinctive sense consciousness, since all its consciousnesses are mind-consciousness. Hence it is called the mind-consciousness process. Here a “process” means the arising of consciousnesses in sequence at the respective door, such as five-door adverting followed by eye-consciousness and the subsequent moments.
paragraphs.M04-body-P018-S03:
Six modes of presentation of objects (visayappavatti).
1. Very great object (atimahantārammaṇa): a very large number of consciousness moments can be counted from its appearance at the corresponding door to its cessation. This is the course with registration (tadārammaṇavāra).
2. Great object (mahantārammaṇa): many consciousness moments can be counted from its appearance at the corresponding door to its cessation. This is the course with impulsion (javanavāra).
3. Slight object (parittārammaṇa): few consciousness moments can be counted from its appearance at the corresponding door to its cessation. This is the course ending in determining (voṭṭhabbanavāra).

M04-body-P019.title: The remaining modes of presentation and the objects of insight knowledge

paragraphs.M04-body-P019-S01:
4. Very slight object (atiparittārammaṇa): very few consciousness moments can be counted from its appearance at the corresponding door to its cessation. (In the futile course, moghavāra, no process consciousness arises and only the life-continuum continues its function.) The four preceding kinds pertain to the five sense doors.
5. Clear object (vibhūtārammaṇa): an object that appears clearly. This is the course with registration.
6. Obscure object (avibhūtārammaṇa): an object that does not appear clearly. This is the course with impulsion. These two pertain to the mind-door.
paragraphs.M04-body-P019-S02: There are thus six modes of presentation. These are the sets of six to know beforehand. If you wish to practise meditation on mentality, first learn the consciousnesses comprised in the six consciousness elements and their associated mental factors. We will begin with consciousnesses that can arise in your own continuum and can therefore serve as objects to discern and investigate in insight.
paragraphs.M04-body-P019-S03: Types of consciousness that are objects of insight knowledge. The Buddha taught four ultimate realities: consciousness, mental factors, materiality and Nibbāna. If you wish to realize Nibbāna, the fourth ultimate reality, first strive to know consciousness, mental factors and materiality, the first three ultimate realities, together with dependent origination, the causal relationship through which consciousness, mental factors and materiality arise repeatedly…

M04-body-P020.title: Consciousness and the kinds of unwholesome consciousness

paragraphs.M04-body-P020-S01: … Only when one can thoroughly discern in insight those consciousnesses, mental factors and material phenomena together with their conditions under the three characteristics can the knowledge of the noble path and fruition, arising at the culmination of mature insight, penetrate and see Nibbāna, the fourth ultimate reality. Of these ultimate realities, consciousness and mental factors are called mentality. We will now present the consciousnesses that are objects of insight knowledge.
paragraphs.M04-body-P020-S02: Consciousness (citta) is the phenomenon capable of knowing an object. “Knowing” here means apprehending the object: “Vijānanaṃ ārammaṇassa upaladdhi.” (Mūlaṭīkā, vol. 1, p. 87.) When you can take eye-sensitivity as object at the level of ultimate reality, you are said to know eye-sensitivity. Until you can take eye-sensitivity as object, you cannot be said to know it. Understand the other cases in the same way.
paragraphs.M04-body-P020-S03: Twelve unwholesome consciousnesses. There are four classes of consciousness: sense-sphere, fine-material-sphere, immaterial-sphere and supramundane. Among the fifty-four sense-sphere consciousnesses are the following twelve unwholesome consciousnesses.
paragraphs.M04-body-P020-S04:
Eight greed-rooted consciousnesses.
1. One consciousness accompanied by gladness (somanassa), associated with wrong view and unprompted.
2. One consciousness accompanied by gladness (somanassa), associated with wrong view and prompted.

paragraphs.M04-body-P021-S01:
3. One consciousness accompanied by equanimity, associated with wrong view, and unprompted.
4. One consciousness accompanied by equanimity, associated with wrong view, and prompted.
5. One consciousness accompanied by gladness, dissociated from wrong view, and unprompted.
6. One consciousness accompanied by gladness, dissociated from wrong view, and prompted.
7. One consciousness accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from wrong view, and unprompted.
8. One consciousness accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from wrong view, and prompted.
paragraphs.M04-body-P021-S02: Thus there are eight greed-rooted consciousnesses.
paragraphs.M04-body-P021-S03:
Somanassasahagata: arising together with gladness.
Upekkhāsahagata: arising together with equanimity.
Diṭṭhigatasampayutta: associated with wrong acceptance, that is, wrong view.
Diṭṭhigatavippayutta: dissociated from wrong view.
Sasaṅkhārika: prompted, occurring with prompting.
Asaṅkhārika: unprompted, occurring without prompting.
paragraphs.M04-body-P021-S05:
1. One consciousness accompanied by displeasure, associated with aversion, and unprompted.
2. One consciousness accompanied by displeasure, associated with aversion, and prompted.
paragraphs.M04-body-P021-S06:
Domanassasahagata: arising together with displeasure, the unpleasant feeling of mind.
Paṭighasampayutta: associated with harshness and aggression of mind, that is, hatred.

M04-body-P022.title: Delusion-rooted consciousness and rootless unwholesome resultants

paragraphs.M04-body-P022-S02:
1. One consciousness accompanied by equanimity and associated with doubt.
2. One consciousness accompanied by equanimity and associated with restlessness.
paragraphs.M04-body-P022-S03:
Vicikicchāsampayutta: associated with doubt.
Uddhaccasampayutta: associated with restlessness, agitation of the mind.
paragraphs.M04-body-P022-S04:
1. Eight consciousnesses with greed as root.
2. Two consciousnesses with hatred as root.
3. Two consciousnesses with delusion as root.
paragraphs.M04-body-P022-S05: Thus there are twelve unwholesome consciousnesses.
paragraphs.M04-body-P022-S06: Eighteen rootless consciousnesses. Seven unwholesome-resultant consciousnesses
paragraphs.M04-body-P022-S07:
1. One unwholesome-resultant eye-consciousness accompanied by equanimity.
2. One unwholesome-resultant ear-consciousness accompanied by equanimity.
3. One unwholesome-resultant nose-consciousness accompanied by equanimity.
4. One unwholesome-resultant tongue-consciousness accompanied by equanimity.
5. One unwholesome-resultant body-consciousness accompanied by bodily pain.
6. One unwholesome-resultant receiving consciousness accompanied by equanimity.
7. One unwholesome-resultant investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity.
paragraphs.M04-body-P022-S08:
Dukkhasahagata: arising together with bodily pain.
Sampaṭicchanacitta: consciousness that arises in the role of receiving the object.
Santīraṇacitta: consciousness that arises in the role of investigating the object.

M04-body-P023.title: Rootless wholesome resultants and rootless functional consciousness

paragraphs.M04-body-P023-S01: These seven consciousnesses are results of past unwholesome kamma. They arise in your continuum when you encounter undesirable objects. Remember that encounters with the various undesirable objects in this life are due to past unwholesome kamma. This is a point to bear in mind.
paragraphs.M04-body-P023-S03:
1. One rootless wholesome-resultant eye-consciousness accompanied by equanimity.
2. One rootless wholesome-resultant ear-consciousness accompanied by equanimity.
3. One rootless wholesome-resultant nose-consciousness accompanied by equanimity.
4. One rootless wholesome-resultant tongue-consciousness accompanied by equanimity.
5. One rootless wholesome-resultant body-consciousness accompanied by bodily pleasure.
6. One rootless wholesome-resultant receiving consciousness accompanied by equanimity.
7. One rootless wholesome-resultant investigating consciousness accompanied by gladness.
8. One rootless wholesome-resultant investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity.
paragraphs.M04-body-P023-S04:
These eight consciousnesses are results of past wholesome kamma. They arise in your continuum through past wholesome kamma when you encounter desirable objects.
Sukhasahagata: arising together with bodily pleasure.
paragraphs.M04-body-P023-S06:
1. One five-door-adverting consciousness accompanied by equanimity.
2. One mind-door-adverting consciousness accompanied by equanimity.
3. One smile-producing consciousness accompanied by gladness.

M04-body-P024.title: Eighteen rootless consciousnesses and beautiful sense-sphere consciousnesses

paragraphs.M04-body-P024-S01:
Five-door adverting (pañcadvārāvajjana): consciousness that adverts to an object appearing at one of the five doors.
Mind-door adverting (manodvārāvajjana): consciousness that adverts to an object appearing at the mind-door.
Smile-producing consciousness (hasituppādacitta): consciousness that produces a smile in the continuum of arahants.
paragraphs.M04-body-P024-S02: These three merely advert when a door encounters an object, or produce a smile. They have no power to produce a result, so they are called functional consciousnesses (kiriyacitta).
paragraphs.M04-body-P024-S03:
1. Seven unwholesome-resultant consciousnesses.
2. Eight rootless wholesome-resultant consciousnesses.
3. Three rootless functional consciousnesses.
paragraphs.M04-body-P024-S04: These eighteen consciousnesses are associated with none of the roots greed, hatred, delusion, non-greed, non-hatred and non-delusion. Hence they are called rootless. The remaining consciousnesses, apart from the unwholesome and the rootless, are beautiful and are called beautiful consciousnesses (sobhanacitta). There are fifty-nine in the concise enumeration and ninety-one in the detailed enumeration.
paragraphs.M04-body-P024-S05: Twenty-four beautiful sense-sphere consciousnesses. Eight great wholesome consciousnesses
paragraphs.M04-body-P024-S06:
1. One consciousness accompanied by gladness, associated with knowledge, and unprompted.
2. One consciousness accompanied by gladness, associated with knowledge, and prompted.
3. One consciousness accompanied by equanimity, associated with knowledge, and unprompted.

M04-body-P025.title: Great wholesome and great resultant consciousnesses

paragraphs.M04-body-P025-S01:
4. One consciousness accompanied by equanimity, associated with knowledge, and prompted.
5. One consciousness accompanied by gladness, dissociated from knowledge, and unprompted.
6. One consciousness accompanied by gladness, dissociated from knowledge, and prompted.
7. One consciousness accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from knowledge, and unprompted.
8. One consciousness accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from knowledge, and prompted.
paragraphs.M04-body-P025-S02: These eight are wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses. Generally they can produce favourable results in the eleven sense-sphere planes. In your continuum as a worldling, the consciousnesses developing tranquillity as far as access concentration and those developing insight before and after the noble path belong to this class of wholesome sense-sphere consciousness. Because their range is wide, they are also called great wholesome consciousnesses.
paragraphs.M04-body-P025-S04: 1. One consciousness accompanied by gladness, associated with knowledge, and unprompted.
paragraphs.M04-body-P025-S05:
Pe.
8. One consciousness accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from knowledge, and prompted.
paragraphs.M04-body-P025-S06: They parallel the eight great wholesome consciousnesses, differing only in being resultant rather than wholesome. The eight great resultant consciousnesses are results of great wholesome kamma. One of them performs rebirth-linking, life-continuum and death in the continuum of a three-rooted or two-rooted worldling. During life, when various sense objects are encountered, all eight can perform registration, continuing to take the same object after sense-sphere impulsion, and…

M04-body-P026.title: Great functional consciousnesses and the sense-sphere total

paragraphs.M04-body-P026-S01: … arise as appropriate in the continuum of beings in the sense sphere. Sense-sphere objects here are sense-sphere consciousness and mental factors and the twenty-eight kinds of materiality, when desirable and pleasing.
paragraphs.M04-body-P026-S03: 1. One consciousness accompanied by gladness, associated with knowledge, and unprompted.
paragraphs.M04-body-P026-S04:
Pe.
8. One consciousness accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from knowledge, and prompted.
paragraphs.M04-body-P026-S05: The great functional consciousnesses likewise have eight kinds corresponding to the great wholesome consciousnesses. They are the consciousnesses of arahants when giving, observing virtue, and developing tranquillity and insight. Here tranquillity extends to access concentration. The consciousnesses with which arahants practise giving, virtue, tranquillity and insight have no power to generate results, so they are called functional, merely performing their work.
paragraphs.M04-body-P026-S06: The eight great wholesome, eight great resultant and eight great functional consciousnesses make twenty-four beautiful sense-sphere consciousnesses. They usually operate and arise in the sense sphere.
paragraphs.M04-body-P026-S07: Twelve unwholesome, eighteen rootless, and twenty-four beautiful sense-sphere consciousnesses. Total: fifty-four. They are called sense-sphere consciousnesses because they arise mostly in the eleven sense-sphere planes. Sense-sphere mentality comprises these fifty-four consciousnesses…

M04-body-P027.title: Sense-sphere objects of insight and five fine-material wholesome consciousnesses

paragraphs.M04-body-P027-S01: … and the fifty-two mental factors associated with them as appropriate. If you are a three-rooted worldling, the sense-sphere consciousnesses that can arise in your continuum and serve as objects of your insight knowledge are:
paragraphs.M04-body-P027-S02:
1. Twelve unwholesome consciousnesses.
2. Seventeen rootless consciousnesses, excluding smile-producing consciousness.
3. Eight great wholesome consciousnesses.
4. Eight great resultant consciousnesses.
paragraphs.M04-body-P027-S04: Fifteen fine-material-sphere consciousnesses. Five wholesome consciousnesses
paragraphs.M04-body-P027-S05:
1. Wholesome first jhāna consciousness arises with 5 factors: applied thought, sustained thought, joy, pleasure, one-pointedness.
2. Wholesome second jhāna consciousness arises with 4 factors: sustained thought, joy, pleasure, one-pointedness.
3. Wholesome third jhāna consciousness arises with 3 factors: joy, pleasure, one-pointedness.
4. Wholesome fourth jhāna consciousness arises with 2 factors: pleasure, one-pointedness.
5. Wholesome fifth jhāna consciousness arises with 2 factors: equanimity, one-pointedness.

M04-body-P028.title: Fine-material consciousness and wholesome immaterial consciousnesses

paragraphs.M04-body-P028-S01: Thus there are five wholesome fine-material consciousnesses by the fivefold reckoning of jhāna. There are also five corresponding fine-material resultant consciousnesses. These arise only in the respective fine-material planes in the continuum of brahmās, performing rebirth-linking, life-continuum and death. Likewise, if arahants attain fine-material jhānas, these jhānas are called functional because they cannot produce a result. There are five fine-material functional consciousnesses. In all there are fifteen fine-material-sphere consciousnesses.
paragraphs.M04-body-P028-S02: If you attain a wholesome fine-material jhāna, that jhāna is among the objects of your insight knowledge. If you attain all four fine-material jhānas by the fourfold reckoning or all five by the fivefold reckoning, all of them are among the objects of your insight knowledge.
paragraphs.M04-body-P028-S03: Twelve immaterial-sphere consciousnesses. Four wholesome consciousnesses
paragraphs.M04-body-P028-S04:
1. Wholesome consciousness of the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana) takes the concept of unbounded space as object.
2. Wholesome consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana) takes the consciousness of the base of infinite space as object.
3. Wholesome consciousness of the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) takes…

M04-body-P029.title: Immaterial consciousness and the scope of discernment for jhāna attainments

paragraphs.M04-body-P029-S01: … the absence of the consciousness of the base of infinite space, the concept of absence (natthibhāvapaññatti), as object.
paragraphs.M04-body-P029-S02: 4. Wholesome consciousness of the base of neither perception nor non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana): it cannot be said to have perception or to be without perception. Clear, gross perception is absent, and only exceedingly subtle perception remains.
paragraphs.M04-body-P029-S03: There are four wholesome immaterial-sphere consciousnesses. Their resultants are also of four kinds and arise only in the continuum of brahmās of the corresponding immaterial planes. If arahants attain the immaterial jhānas, those consciousnesses are called functional because they have no power to produce a result. The eight wholesome and resultant immaterial consciousnesses and the four functional immaterial consciousnesses make twelve. If you attain the immaterial jhānas, all four are also objects of your insight knowledge. Thus the maximum number of consciousnesses that can arise in your continuum and serve as objects of insight knowledge if you have attained jhāna is:
paragraphs.M04-body-P029-S04:
1. Forty-five sense-sphere consciousnesses.
2. Five wholesome fine-material jhāna consciousnesses by the fivefold reckoning.
3. Four wholesome immaterial jhāna consciousnesses.
paragraphs.M04-body-P029-S05: Total: fifty-four consciousnesses. These are what sense-sphere worldlings and trainees who have attained jhāna use insight knowledge to…

M04-body-P030.title: Eighty-one mundane and eight supramundane consciousnesses

paragraphs.M04-body-P030-S01: … discern. They are the phenomena that serve as objects of insight knowledge.
paragraphs.M04-body-P030-S02: Reckoning comprehensively for worldlings, trainees and those beyond training in the sense, fine-material and immaterial realms, eighty-one mundane consciousnesses serve as objects of insight knowledge. They consist of fifty-four sense-sphere, fifteen fine-material and twelve immaterial-sphere consciousnesses. They are called mundane because they operate and arise in the world of thirty-one planes.
paragraphs.M04-body-P030-S03: Eight supramundane consciousnesses in brief. Four noble path consciousnesses
paragraphs.M04-body-P030-S04:
1. Stream-entry path consciousness.
2. Once-return path consciousness.
3. Non-return path consciousness.
4. Arahantship path consciousness.
paragraphs.M04-body-P030-S05: Thus there are four path consciousnesses.
paragraphs.M04-body-P030-S07:
1. Stream-entry fruition consciousness.
2. Once-return fruition consciousness.
3. Non-return fruition consciousness.
4. Arahantship fruition consciousness.
paragraphs.M04-body-P030-S08: Thus there are four fruition consciousnesses. They are the resultants of the corresponding noble paths.

paragraphs.M04-body-P031-S01: After apprehending the mundane mentality that can arise in your continuum, that is, consciousness and mental factors, and the material phenomena presented in the section on materiality, seek their conditions. When you thoroughly develop insight into mentality and materiality together with their conditions under the three characteristics, the knowledge of the noble path and fruition arises at the culmination of insight.
paragraphs.M04-body-P031-S02: If one reaches a noble path while discerning sense-sphere mentality or material phenomena, that noble path and fruition are associated with first jhāna. (Abhidhamma Commentary, vol. 1, pp. 272–273.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P031-S03:
Lokuttaramaggo hi appanaṃ appatto nāma natthi, tasmā rūpaṃ sammasitvā vuṭṭhitassa aṭṭhaṅgiko somanassasahagatamaggo hoti. (Abhidhamma Commentary, vol. 1, p. 274.)
A supramundane path always reaches absorption. Thus, for one emerging after discerning materiality, the path has eight factors and is accompanied by gladness.
paragraphs.M04-body-P031-S04: Thus when the noble path is reached by discerning sense-sphere mentality or materiality, there are eight path factors, seven awakening factors and five jhāna factors. These are factors of supramundane jhāna. This is called the supramundane path associated with first jhāna.
paragraphs.M04-body-P031-S06: 1. If one reaches a noble path while discerning the mentality of first jhāna, that path and fruition are associated with first jhāna.

paragraphs.M04-body-P032-S01:
2. If one reaches a noble path while discerning the mentality of second jhāna, that path and fruition are associated with second jhāna.
3. If one reaches a noble path while discerning the mentality of third jhāna, that path and fruition are associated with third jhāna.
4. If one reaches a noble path while discerning the mentality of fourth jhāna, that path and fruition are associated with fourth jhāna.
5. If one reaches a noble path while discerning the mentality of fifth jhāna, that path and fruition are associated with fifth jhāna.
paragraphs.M04-body-P032-S02: If one reaches the noble path while discerning sense-sphere mentality or materiality, the path and fruition are associated with first jhāna. Thus:
paragraphs.M04-body-P032-S03:
1. Five stream-entry path consciousnesses and five stream-entry fruition consciousnesses.
2. Five once-return path consciousnesses and five once-return fruition consciousnesses.
3. Five non-return path consciousnesses and five non-return fruition consciousnesses.
4. Five arahantship path consciousnesses and five arahantship fruition consciousnesses.
paragraphs.M04-body-P032-S04: This gives forty supramundane consciousnesses in detail. In brief, eighty-one mundane and eight supramundane consciousnesses make eighty-nine, one short of ninety. In detail, eighty-one plus forty make one hundred and twenty-one by the fivefold reckoning of jhāna.

M04-body-P033.title: Part 2. What to know about mental factors

paragraphs.M04-body-P033-S01: By its characteristic of knowing or apprehending an object, consciousness is of one kind. Yet because the mental factors arising with it in each moment vary, consciousness is classified into many kinds. Neither consciousness nor mental factors can arise separately from the other. At every moment they arise together in a group. The Great Subcommentary to the Visuddhimagga calls the group of consciousness and mental factors arising in one moment an immaterial group (arūpakalāpa), or mental group (nāmakalāpa). (Mahāṭīkā, vol. 2, p. 235.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P033-S02: Four characteristics of mental factors associated with consciousness
paragraphs.M04-body-P033-S03:
1. Ekuppāda: arising together with consciousness.
2. Ekanirodha: ceasing together with consciousness.
3. Ekārammaṇa: taking the same object as consciousness.

M04-body-P034.title: The fifty-two mental factors and the universals

paragraphs.M04-body-P034-S01: 4. Ekavatthuka: sharing the same base as consciousness.
paragraphs.M04-body-P034-S02: These are the four characteristics of association. When a mental factor is associated with consciousness in a sense or fine-material plane, all four are present. In the immaterial planes the shared base is absent because there is no material base. There are fifty-two mental factors.
paragraphs.M04-body-P034-S03:
1. Seven universals (sabbacittasādhāraṇa), common to all consciousnesses.
2. Six occasionals (pakiṇṇaka), associated only on certain occasions.
3. Fourteen unwholesome mental factors, associated with unwholesome consciousnesses.
4. Twenty-five beautiful mental factors, associated with beautiful consciousnesses.
paragraphs.M04-body-P034-S05: Seven universals: mental factors associated with every consciousness
paragraphs.M04-body-P034-S06:
1. Contact (phassa): characterized by touching the object, with the function of bringing object and consciousness together.
2. Feeling (vedanā): experiencing the flavour of the object.

M04-body-P035.title: The seven universal mental factors, continued

paragraphs.M04-body-P035-S01:
3. Perception (saññā): marking the object.
4. Volition (cetanā): leading and urging the associated consciousness and mental factors toward the object.
5. One-pointedness (ekaggatā): convergence of consciousness on one object, steadiness, and keeping the associated phenomena from scattering.
6. Life faculty (jīvita): maintaining the associated consciousness and mental factors, the vitality of mentality.
7. Attention (manasikāra): directing and driving the associated phenomena toward the object, bringing the object to mind.
paragraphs.M04-body-P035-S02: Note. Consciousness and the mental factors associated with it in a moment are called associated phenomena (sampayuttadhamma). Depending on the occasion and the strength of the mind’s steadiness, one-pointedness is also called the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, the concentration awakening factor, right concentration, access concentration, absorption concentration, and so on. Notice also the mental factor of feeling. It is universal, associated with every consciousness. As long as there is consciousness, there is feeling. Feeling may be bodily pleasure, bodily pain, gladness, displeasure, or equanimity. A consciousness devoid of feeling, unassociated with feeling…

paragraphs.M04-body-P036-S01: … cannot occur according to the Buddha’s teaching. Feeling ceases. The view that feeling ceases while the knowing consciousness does not is not the Buddhist view.
paragraphs.M04-body-P036-S02: Six occasional mental factors (pakiṇṇaka), associated on certain occasions
paragraphs.M04-body-P036-S03:
1. Applied thought (vitakka): placing consciousness and its associates on the object, directing the mind to it.
2. Sustained thought (vicāra): examining the object repeatedly, continuing to hold it.
3. Decision (adhimokkha): making a decision regarding the object.
4. Energy (viriya): exertion, effort, and having the strength to press on.
paragraphs.M04-body-P036-S04: Energy is the effort for the associated consciousness and mental factors to arise on an object. On the unwholesome side, there is effort toward greed, hatred and delusion, and so on. On the wholesome side, there is effort toward non-greed, non-hatred and non-delusion, and so on. In concentration there is effort to develop concentration. In insight there is effort to know the four great elements, materiality, mentality, their conditions, and the characteristics of impermanence, suffering and non-self of mentality and materiality together with those conditions.

M04-body-P037.title: Desire and the distinction between applied thought, volition and attention

paragraphs.M04-body-P037-S01: 6. Desire (chanda): wanting the object, wishing to act in relation to it.
paragraphs.M04-body-P037-S02: According to the occasion, understand this as the wish for greed, hatred, delusion, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, concentration or wisdom in relation to an object. Wishing to see, hear, smell, taste, touch or know is also wishing to act in relation to the object.
paragraphs.M04-body-P037-S03: These six are associated with only some consciousnesses. As they accompany them on particular occasions, one or another as the case may be, they are called occasionals. The seven universals and six occasionals together are the thirteen ethically variable mental factors (aññasamāna). They are associated as appropriate with unwholesome and rootless consciousnesses, classed as non-beautiful, and with the fifty-nine beautiful consciousnesses in brief or ninety-one in detail. They are thus shared by both the wholesome and unwholesome sides.
paragraphs.M04-body-P037-S05: Applied thought places the associated phenomena on the object. Volition brings into engagement with the object the associated phenomena that applied thought has placed there. Attention…

M04-body-P038.title: The four unwholesome universals and the greed group

paragraphs.M04-body-P038-S01: … directs the associated phenomena straight toward the object, driving them toward it.
paragraphs.M04-body-P038-S02: Fourteen unwholesome mental factors. Four unwholesome universals
paragraphs.M04-body-P038-S03:
1. Delusion (moha): not knowing the true nature of the object, knowing it wrongly.
2. Shamelessness (ahirika): absence of shame about misconduct or unwholesome states such as greed, hatred and delusion.
3. Moral recklessness (anottappa): absence of dread of misconduct or unwholesome states such as greed, hatred and delusion.
4. Restlessness (uddhacca): agitation and instability of mind regarding the object.
paragraphs.M04-body-P038-S04: Since these four always accompany every unwholesome consciousness, they are called unwholesome universals.
paragraphs.M04-body-P038-S05: Three mental factors in the greed group
paragraphs.M04-body-P038-S06:
5. Greed (lobha): taking an object as “mine”, craving it and clinging to it.
6. Wrong view (diṭṭhi): holding and believing the object to be permanent, pleasant, self, and beautiful. It is a mistaken view, a mistaken conviction.

paragraphs.M04-body-P039-S01: 7. Conceit (māna): the mind exalting itself, “I, I”, being proud and wanting to be superior.
paragraphs.M04-body-P039-S03:
Paramatthato avijjamānesu itthipurisādīsu javati, vijjamānesupi khandhādīsu na javatīti avijjā. (Abhidhamma Commentary, vol. 2, p. 127; Visuddhimagga, vol. 2, p. 157.)
Ignorance runs toward what does not exist ultimately, such as women and men, and does not run toward what does exist, such as the aggregates.
paragraphs.M04-body-P039-S04: Delusion is also called ignorance. When one can analyse with the right view of insight the animate and inanimate world in the thirty-one planes down to ultimate reality, one knows that:
paragraphs.M04-body-P039-S05:
1. There are only groups of material phenomena.
2. There are only groups of mental phenomena.
3. There are only groups of mentality and materiality, the five aggregates, twelve bases or eighteen elements. This is correct knowledge, called knowledge of delimiting mentality and materiality.
4. There are only groups of causes and groups of effects. This is also correct knowledge, called knowledge of apprehending conditions.
paragraphs.M04-body-P039-S06: Materiality, mentality, causes and effects are called conditioned phenomena. They are impermanent because they arise and cease, and suffering because arising and ceasing constantly oppress them. They are all non-self, since there is no solid, indestructible self that persists as a core…

paragraphs.M04-body-P040-S01: … They are also only unattractive phenomena, liable to arouse disenchantment. Thus it is correct to know those conditioned phenomena as only impermanent, suffering, non-self and unattractive. These are knowledges of insight.
paragraphs.M04-body-P040-S02: If one knows animate and inanimate things in the thirty-one planes as groups of materiality, mentality, or mentality and materiality, that is, as the five aggregates, twelve bases or eighteen elements, as groups of causes and effects, or as groups of impermanent, suffering, non-self and unattractive phenomena, that knowing is correct knowing, right view or knowledge.
paragraphs.M04-body-P040-S03: If, instead of knowing in accordance with their actual nature, one knows them as men, women, persons, beings, devas or brahmās, as a life, soul, consciousness or self, as gold, silver, trees, water, land, forests or mountains, or knows those animate and inanimate things in the contrary way as permanent, pleasant, self and beautiful, that mistaken knowing is called ignorance or delusion.
paragraphs.M04-body-P040-S04: To clarify the difference between ignorance, or delusion, and wrong view, two kinds of clinging to self important in insight practice will be explained.

M04-body-P041.title: Two kinds of clinging to self

paragraphs.M04-body-P041-S01: Broadly, there are two kinds of clinging to self: clinging based on ordinary worldly usage (lokavohāra), and clinging based on the view of self posited by proponents of wrong view outside the dispensation. (Majjhima Nikāya Subcommentary, vol. 1, pp. 365–366.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P041-S02: 1. Clinging to self by worldly convention: taking living things as men, women, persons, beings, devas, brahmās, buffaloes, cattle, animals and so on, and inanimate things as gold, silver, fields, gardens, houses, trees, water, land, forests, mountains and so on.
paragraphs.M04-body-P041-S03: When you can apprehend external mentality and materiality, direct insight knowledge toward the external animate world. You will see for yourself by right view that what is called external living beings are only groups of materiality, mentality, mentality and materiality, causes, effects, impermanent, suffering, non-self and unattractive phenomena.
paragraphs.M04-body-P041-S04: Direct insight knowledge also toward the external inanimate world. Use wisdom to discern the four great elements in external inanimate things such as gold and silver. On seeing minute material clusters, you will see only successive temperature-produced materiality due to fire, or temperature, in each cluster. Where there is sound, there are temperature-produced sound nonads. Thus if you know inanimate things as groups of temperature-produced materiality, or where there is sound…

M04-body-P042.title: Clinging by convention and clinging by wrong view

paragraphs.M04-body-P042-S01: … as groups of temperature-produced sound nonads, that knowing is correct. If one knows them as gold, silver and so forth, that knowing is mistaken. It is ignorance, or delusion.
paragraphs.M04-body-P042-S02: If one fails to know living beings as groups of materiality, mentality, causes and effects, the conditioned phenomena, or as groups of impermanent, suffering, non-self and unattractive phenomena, and knows them as men, women, persons, beings, devas and brahmās, that knowing is mistaken. It is ignorance or delusion. If one further clings to and believes that men, women, persons, beings, devas and brahmās truly exist just as they are conventionally called, that belief, clinging and mistaken conviction is conventional clinging to self, a wrong view.
paragraphs.M04-body-P042-S03: Likewise, failure to know inanimate objects as groups of materiality and knowing them as gold, silver, diamonds or gems is mistaken knowing, ignorance. If one clings to, believes and accepts that gold, silver, diamonds and gems really exist as they are called in the world, that is clinging to self by worldly convention, a mistaken conviction and wrong view.
paragraphs.M04-body-P042-S04: 2. The view of self (attadiṭṭhi). Broadly, there are two kinds: (a) the view of a supreme self (paramattadiṭṭhi); (b) the view of a living self (jīvattadiṭṭhi).
paragraphs.M04-body-P042-S05: (a) The supreme self: clinging to the idea of a creator self that creates the world and its beings…

M04-body-P043.title: Distinguishing delusion from wrong view, and the hatred group

paragraphs.M04-body-P043-S01:
… is the view of a supreme self.
(b) The view of a living self is the belief and clinging that each being’s continuum contains an enduring life, soul, consciousness or self.
paragraphs.M04-body-P043-S02: Mistakenly knowing a supreme self or living self is ignorance, or delusion. Clinging, believing and mistakenly accepting that such selves actually exist is the view of self, a wrong view.
paragraphs.M04-body-P043-S03: Distinguishing delusion from wrong view in brief
paragraphs.M04-body-P043-S04: Delusion mistakenly knows animate and inanimate things in the thirty-one planes as permanent, pleasant, self and beautiful. Wrong view believes and mistakenly accepts them as permanent, pleasant, self and beautiful. That mistaken knowing is delusion. That mistaken view is wrong view.
paragraphs.M04-body-P043-S05: Four mental factors in the hatred group
paragraphs.M04-body-P043-S06:
8. Hatred (dosa): harshness and roughness of mind, wishing to destroy.
9. Envy (issā): begrudging the property, standing and happiness of others, wishing to be the only one who excels.
10. Stinginess (macchariya): hiding one’s possessions, unwillingness to share them, meanness.

paragraphs.M04-body-P044-S01: 11. Remorse (kukkucca): later distress over having done what is bad, unwholesome or misconduct, or over having omitted what is good, wholesome or good conduct.
paragraphs.M04-body-P044-S02: Two mental factors in the prompted group
paragraphs.M04-body-P044-S03:
12. Sloth (thīna): sluggishness of consciousness, its lack of alertness and vigour.
13. Torpor (middha): sluggishness of the associated mental factors, their lack of alertness and vigour.
paragraphs.M04-body-P044-S04: One mental factor in the delusion group
paragraphs.M04-body-P044-S05:
14. Doubt (vicikicchā), uncertainty concerning:
1. The genuine, fully awakened Buddha.
2. The genuine Dhamma of the fully awakened Buddha.
3. The genuine Saṅgha of noble disciples of the fully awakened Buddha.
4. The three trainings in virtue, concentration and wisdom.
5. Past life, the past aggregates, called the earlier end of saṃsāra.
6. Future life, the future aggregates, called the later end of saṃsāra.
7. Both past and future lives, the two ends of saṃsāra…

M04-body-P045.title: Doubt and the beautiful mental factors

paragraphs.M04-body-P045-S01:
… that is, both the past and future aggregates.
8. The connection of cause and effect, dependent origination.
Doubt is uncertainty regarding these eight subjects. (Abhidhamma, vol. 1, p. 208.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P045-S02: Note. Doubt about kamma and its results is included in doubt about the connection of cause and effect, dependent origination.
paragraphs.M04-body-P045-S04:
(a) Nineteen beautiful universals, common to all beautiful consciousnesses.
(b) Three abstinences.
(c) Two immeasurables.
(d) One faculty of wisdom.
Total: twenty-five.
paragraphs.M04-body-P045-S06:
1. Faith (saddhā): confidence and clarity regarding the eight subjects listed under doubt, that is, trust and conviction. Note. This is a general description. Distinguish the cases as follows:
1. Taking the qualities of the Buddha as object, confidence in those qualities.
2. Taking the qualities of the Dhamma as object, confidence in those qualities.

M04-body-P046.title: Faith, mindfulness, moral shame, moral dread and non-greed

paragraphs.M04-body-P046-S01:
3. Taking the qualities of the Saṅgha as object, confidence in those qualities.
4. In virtue, confidence in the training in virtue. In concentration, confidence in training in jhāna concentration. In wisdom, confidence in training to penetrate the actual nature of ultimate mentality and materiality, and in training to penetrate the four truths.
5. When discerning the past, confidence regarding the past aggregates.
6. When discerning the future, confidence regarding the future aggregates.
7. When discerning both past and future, confidence regarding both sets of aggregates.
8. When discerning the link of cause and effect, dependent origination, confidence in the actual nature of that connection.
paragraphs.M04-body-P046-S02: Understand in this way how confidence varies according to the object discerned.
paragraphs.M04-body-P046-S03:
2. Mindfulness (sati): on an object where mindfulness is established, such as the four establishments of mindfulness, it causes the associated phenomena to sink like a stone instead of floating like a gourd. The mind stands firmly on the object and does not forget it.
3. Moral shame (hiri): shame regarding unwholesome acts and misconduct.
4. Moral dread (ottappa): dread regarding unwholesome acts and misconduct.
5. Non-greed (alobha): the mind does not cling to or crave mundane objects…

paragraphs.M04-body-P047-S01: … and does not take them as “mine”.
paragraphs.M04-body-P047-S02:
6. Non-hatred (adosa): absence of harshness or roughness toward the object, and absence of the wish to destroy.
7. Mental balance (tatramajjhattatā): keeping the mind balanced on its object, without falling into conceit or shrinking through sloth and torpor, so that consciousness and mental factors are neither excessive nor deficient in their functions, and attend to the object evenly.
8. Tranquillity of the mental body (kāyapassaddhi): tranquillity of the mental factors.
9. Tranquillity of consciousness (cittapassaddhi): tranquillity of consciousness.
10. Lightness of the mental body (kāyalahutā): agility and lightness of the mental factors.
11. Lightness of consciousness (cittalahutā): agility and lightness of consciousness.
12. Malleability of the mental body (kāyamudutā): pliancy of the mental factors.
13. Malleability of consciousness (cittamudutā): pliancy of consciousness.
14. Wieldiness of the mental body (kāyakammaññatā): fitness of the mental factors for giving, virtue, meditation and so on, and their smooth functioning. In meditation, discernment proceeds smoothly.
15. Wieldiness of consciousness (cittakammaññatā): fitness of consciousness for giving, virtue, meditation and so on, and its smooth functioning. In meditation, discernment proceeds smoothly.
16. Proficiency of the mental body (kāyapāguññatā): in giving, virtue, meditation and similar wholesome activities…

M04-body-P048.title: Proficiency, rectitude and two kinds of deceit

paragraphs.M04-body-P048-S01: … the mental factors are well trained and skilful, free from the disease of defilements.
paragraphs.M04-body-P048-S02:
17. Proficiency of consciousness (cittapāguññatā): in giving, virtue, meditation and so on, consciousness is well trained and skilful, free from the disease of defilements.
18. Rectitude of the mental body (kāyujukatā): straightness of the mental factors, free from the crookedness of concealment and deceit.
19. Rectitude of consciousness (cittujukatā): straightness of consciousness, free from the crookedness of concealment and deceit.
paragraphs.M04-body-P048-S04:
Santadosapaṭicchādanalakkhaṇā māyā. Asantaguṇasambhāvanalakkhaṇaṃ sāṭheyyaṃ. (Mahāṭīkā, vol. 1, p. 84.)
Asantaguṇappakāsanalakkhaṇaṃ sāṭheyyaṃ. (Mahāṭīkā, vol. 1, p. 128.)
Concealing a fault that is actually present is māyā. Parading or boasting of qualities one does not have is sāṭheyya.

M04-body-P049.title: Abstinences, immeasurables and the faculty of wisdom

paragraphs.M04-body-P049-S02:
1. Right speech: abstaining from the four kinds of verbal misconduct unrelated to livelihood, refraining from verbal misconduct.
2. Right action: abstaining from the three kinds of bodily misconduct unrelated to livelihood, refraining from bodily misconduct.
3. Right livelihood: abstaining from the four kinds of verbal and the three kinds of bodily misconduct connected with livelihood, refraining from such bodily and verbal misconduct.
paragraphs.M04-body-P049-S04:
1. Compassion (karuṇā): taking suffering beings as object, feeling compassion and wishing to rescue them from distress.
2. Appreciative joy (muditā): taking happy beings as object, rejoicing with them and not begrudging their prosperity.
paragraphs.M04-body-P049-S06: 1. The faculty of wisdom, or wisdom: penetrating the actual nature of ultimate phenomena…

M04-body-P050.title: The faculty of wisdom and an important guideline

paragraphs.M04-body-P050-S01: … penetrating the four truths. Wisdom, also called knowledge, non-delusion, right view or investigation of phenomena, is called a faculty because it predominates in knowing the four truths.
paragraphs.M04-body-P050-S02: This completes the twenty-five beautiful mental factors. A beginner distinguishing and apprehending ultimate phenomena with wisdom may start by attending to the individual characteristic or the function. Hence for some mental factors both characteristic and function have been given.
paragraphs.M04-body-P050-S04:
Idhekacco āditova ajjhattaṃ pañcasu khandhesu abhinivisati. Abhinivisitvā te aniccādito passati. Yasmā pana na suddhaajjhattadassanamatteneva maggavuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, bahiddhāpi daṭṭhabbameva. Tasmā parassa khandhepi anupādinnasaṅkhārepi “aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā”ti passati. So kālena ajjhattaṃ sammasati, kālena bahiddhāti.
One practitioner first enters into discernment of the five aggregates internally. Having done so, one sees them as impermanent and so on. Since path knowledge does not arise through seeing only internally, one also discerns the aggregates of others and unappropriated formations externally as impermanent, suffering and non-self. One discerns at times internally and at times externally. (Abhidhamma Commentary, vol. 1, p. 270.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P050-S05:
Aparo āditova rūpe abhinivisati. Abhinivisitvā bhūtarūpañca upādārūpañca paricchinditvā aniccādito passati. Yasmā pana na suddharūpadassanamatteneva vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, arūpampi daṭṭhabbameva. Tasmā taṃ rūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppannaṃ vedanaṃ saññaṃ saṅkhāre viññāṇañca “idaṃ arūpan”ti paricchinditvā aniccādito passati. So kālena rūpaṃ sammasati kālena arūpaṃ.
Another first enters into discernment of materiality. Having done so, one distinguishes the great elements and derived materiality and sees them as impermanent and so on. Since path knowledge does not arise through seeing only materiality, one takes materiality as object, distinguishes the four mental aggregates arising on that object as mentality, and sees them as impermanent and so on. One discerns at times materiality and at times mentality. (Abhidhamma Commentary, vol. 1, p. 271.)

M04-body-P051.title: Discerning internally and externally, materiality and mentality

paragraphs.M04-body-P051-S01: The meaning of the commentary above is as follows. Once a meditator has attained knowledge of distinguishing mentality and materiality and knowledge of apprehending conditions, they may begin insight by discerning the five aggregates internally. They may also begin with the five aggregates externally, including inanimate formations not appropriated by kamma. But discerning only the internal aggregates or only the external aggregates cannot give rise to insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminīvipassanā), which leads directly from conditioned objects to Nibbāna and the noble path. Therefore discern the five aggregates at times internally and at times externally under the three characteristics.
paragraphs.M04-body-P051-S02: Likewise, insight leading to emergence cannot arise if one discerns only materiality or only mentality. At times distinguish with wisdom the great elements and derived materiality at the ultimate level and discern them under the three characteristics. At times distinguish the four mental aggregates, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness, arising with that materiality as object, and discern them under the three characteristics. This is the meaning of the commentary and agrees with the Aparijānana Sutta and similar discourses in the Saṃyutta Nikāya (vol. 2, pp. 249–250).

M04-body-P052.title: The four contemplations and the scope of discernment

paragraphs.M04-body-P052-S01: Whether in the internal or external continuum, discerning only materiality or only mentality cannot lead to the noble path. One must therefore discern both. Countless groups of materiality and mentality arise and cease over a lifetime. They cannot all be discerned individually by number, but all types must be discerned.
paragraphs.M04-body-P052-S02: The meaning is this. When the material phenomena arising concurrently in the body are seen with wisdom, the material clusters appear as tiny particles. All four great elements occur in these clusters, which are many times smaller than a speck of dust. Disciples cannot discern each element in every cluster. They can discern only some (kesāci), a portion. The same applies to derived materiality.
paragraphs.M04-body-P052-S03: In the very short time of a blink, a flash of lightning or a finger snap, mental phenomena can arise in hundreds of thousands of koṭis of consciousness moments. Over a lifetime their number is incalculable. Disciples cannot discern all of them, only a portion. Yet although they cannot discern them exhaustively by number…

M04-body-P053.title: Discerning all types and the four establishments of mindfulness

paragraphs.M04-body-P053-S01: … they must discern all kinds of material clusters, that is, all types of materiality, as listed in the tables in the section on materiality. They must likewise discern all six kinds of cognitive process, beginning with the eye-door process. Countless eye-door processes know visible objects in a lifetime. One cannot discern every occurrence, only a portion. Understand the same of the ear-door and remaining processes. The commentators accordingly explain:
paragraphs.M04-body-P053-S02:
1. Kāyānupassanāmukhena: through contemplation of the body as the entry.
2. Vedanānupassanāmukhena: through contemplation of feeling as the entry.
3. Cittānupassanāmukhena: through contemplation of consciousness as the entry.
4. Dhammānupassanāmukhena: through contemplation of phenomena as the entry.
paragraphs.M04-body-P053-S03: (See Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, vol. 1, p. 245.) Understand the four contemplations as follows.
paragraphs.M04-body-P053-S04:
1. If one takes materiality as primary, apprehends materiality, mentality, causes and effects, the conditioned phenomena, and discerns them in insight, that comes under the establishment of mindfulness in contemplation of the body. In particular, pure-insight practitioners enter insight through the four great elements, taking materiality as primary when apprehending conditioned phenomena, so their contemplation generally falls under this establishment of mindfulness.
2. Of the three ways of beginning meditation on mentality, if one takes feeling as primary, apprehends materiality, mentality, causes and effects, the conditioned phenomena, and discerns them in insight, that comes under the establishment of mindfulness in contemplation of feeling.

M04-body-P054.title: Entrances to mindfulness and how the tranquillity practitioner begins

paragraphs.M04-body-P054-S01:
3. If one takes knowing consciousness as primary, apprehends materiality, mentality, causes and effects, the conditioned phenomena, and discerns them in insight, that comes under the establishment of mindfulness in contemplation of consciousness.
4. If one takes contact as primary, apprehends materiality, mentality, causes and effects, the conditioned phenomena, and discerns them in insight, that comes under the establishment of mindfulness in contemplation of phenomena.
