Discernment by the five aggregates, twelve bases, eighteen elements and so forth also comes under this establishment of mindfulness. (See Abhidhamma Commentary, vol. 2, p. 273.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P054-S02: Of the three ways of apprehending mentality, beginning with feeling to apprehend and discern conditioned phenomena is contemplation of feeling. Beginning with knowing consciousness is contemplation of consciousness. Beginning with contact is contemplation of phenomena.
paragraphs.M04-body-P054-S03: When moving on to purification of view, one who takes tranquillity as the vehicle may begin practice with either mentality or materiality. If beginning with mentality, first apprehend the jhāna factors and the phenomena associated with jhāna. Then apprehend the heart-base as their support, together with the great elements and derived materiality. (See Visuddhimagga, vol. 2, p. 222.) Then continue to apprehend the sense-sphere mental phenomena called ripened formations and the remaining material phenomena…

M04-body-P055.title: Beginning the apprehension of mentality with feeling

paragraphs.M04-body-P055-S01: … Likewise, the pure-insight practitioner must continue with sense-sphere mental phenomena after practising the materiality meditation subject. Both the tranquillity-vehicle and pure-insight practitioners, when wishing to apprehend sense-sphere mentality, must first develop and apprehend materiality, following the instruction below and the Visuddhimagga commentary cited on Burmese pages 2–4:
paragraphs.M04-body-P055-S02:
Pariggahite rūpakammaṭṭhāne — when the meditation subject of materiality has been apprehended. (Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, vol. 1, p. 280.)
Tasmiṃ ārammaṇe — on that object. (Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, vol. 1, p. 280.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P055-S03:
Tasmā taṃ rūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppannaṃ vedanaṃ saññaṃ saṅkhāre viññāṇañca “idaṃ arūpan”ti paricchinditvā aniccādito passati. (Abhidhamma Commentary, vol. 1, p. 271.)
Thus one delimits feeling, perception, formations and consciousness that arise taking that materiality as object as “this is mentality”, and sees them as impermanent and so on.
paragraphs.M04-body-P055-S04: In accordance with that guideline, begin with the mental phenomena that arise taking those very material phenomena as object. When apprehending them, take particular care to follow the guidelines below.
paragraphs.M04-body-P055-S06: Yassa vedanā pākaṭā hoti, so “na kevalaṃ vedanāva uppajjati. Tāya saddhiṃ tadevārammaṇaṃ phusamāno phassopi uppajjati, sañjānanamānā saññāpi, cetayamānā cetanāpi, vijānanamānaṃ viññāṇampi uppajjatī”ti phassapañcamakeyeva pariggaṇhāti. (Dīgha Nikāya Commentary, vol. 2, p. 314; Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, vol. 1, p. 280; Abhidhamma Commentary, vol. 2, p. 252.)

M04-body-P056.title: Apprehending the five when beginning with feeling or consciousness

paragraphs.M04-body-P056-S01: One to whom feeling is prominent should attend thus: “Feeling does not arise alone. Contact touching that very object also arises with it. Perception marking that object arises. Volition leading and urging the associated phenomena toward that object arises. Consciousness distinguishing or knowing that object also arises.” Apprehend the five phenomena with contact as the fifth (phassapañcamaka). (Dīgha Nikāya Commentary, vol. 2, p. 314; Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, vol. 1, p. 280; Abhidhamma Commentary, vol. 2, p. 252.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P056-S03: Yassa viññāṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, so “na kevalaṃ viññāṇameva uppajjati. Tena saddhiṃ tadevārammaṇaṃ phusamāno phassopi uppajjati, anubhavamānā vedanāpi, sañjānanamānā saññāpi, cetayamānā cetanāpi uppajjatī”ti phassapañcamakeyeva pariggaṇhāti. (Dīgha Nikāya Commentary, vol. 2, p. 314; Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, vol. 1, pp. 280–281; Abhidhamma Commentary, vol. 2, p. 252.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P056-S04: One to whom knowing consciousness is prominent should attend thus: “Consciousness does not arise alone. Contact touching that very object also arises with it. Feeling experiencing the flavour of that object arises. Perception marking it arises. Volition leading and urging the associated phenomena toward it also arises.” Apprehend the five phenomena with contact as the fifth…

M04-body-P057.title: Beginning with contact and apprehending all mental phenomena

paragraphs.M04-body-P057-S01: … those very phenomena. (Dīgha Nikāya Commentary, vol. 2, p. 314; Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, vol. 1, pp. 280–281; Abhidhamma Commentary, vol. 2, p. 252.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P057-S03: Yassa phasso pākaṭo hoti, so “na kevalaṃ phassova uppajjati. Tena saddhiṃ tadevārammaṇaṃ anubhavamānā vedanāpi uppajjati, sañjānanamānā saññāpi, cetayamānā cetanāpi, vijānanamānaṃ viññāṇampi uppajjatī”ti phassapañcamakeyeva pariggaṇhāti. (Dīgha Nikāya Commentary, vol. 2, p. 314; Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, vol. 1, p. 280; Abhidhamma Commentary, vol. 2, p. 252.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P057-S04: One to whom contact is prominent should attend thus: “Contact does not arise alone. Feeling experiencing that very object, tasting its flavour, also arises with it. Perception marking the object arises. Volition leading and urging the associated phenomena toward that object arises. Consciousness distinguishing or knowing that object also arises.” Apprehend the five phenomena with contact as the fifth. (Dīgha Nikāya Commentary, vol. 2, p. 314; Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, vol. 1, p. 280; Abhidhamma Commentary, vol. 2, p. 252.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P057-S06:
Evaṃ tassa tasseva pākaṭabhāvepi “sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, abhiññeyyan”ti, “sabbañca kho, bhikkhave, abhijānan”ti ca evamādivacanato sabbe sammasanupagā dhammā pariggahetabbāti dassento “tattha yassā”tiādimāha. Tattha phassapañcamakeyevāti avadhāraṇaṃ tadantogadhattā taggahaṇeneva gahitattā catunnaṃ arūpakkhandhānaṃ. Phassapañcamakaggahaṇaṃ…
Although these phenomena become evident to the meditator in those ways, the Blessed One taught, “Bhikkhus, all is to be directly known,” and “Bhikkhus, when directly knowing all…”. Therefore all associated phenomena should be apprehended. To make this clear, the explanation begins with “Tattha yassa”. Where it names only the five with contact as the fifth, it is an exposition by way of the principal phenomena, since those phenomena embrace the four mental aggregates…

M04-body-P058.title: Why the five with contact as the fifth are named

paragraphs.M04-body-P058-S01:
… hi tassa sabbacittuppādasādhāraṇabhāvato, tattha ca phassacetanāggahaṇena sabbasaṅkhārakkhandhadhammasaṅgaho cetanāpadhānattā tesaṃ. Tathā hi suttantabhājanīye saṅkhārakkhandhavibhaṅge “cakkhusamphassajā cetanā”tiādinā cetanāva vibhattā, itare pana khandhā sarūpeneva gahitā.
… Of these, contact and volition belong to the formations aggregate. Among the associated phenomena, the formations aggregate may be presented by way of volition, since volition is foremost among them. In the sutta method of presenting the formations aggregate, as in the six classes of volition beginning with volition concerning visible form, volition alone is named. The other aggregates are presented under their own names. (Majjhima Nikāya Subcommentary, vol. 1, p. 370.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P058-S02: Even though contact, feeling or knowing consciousness is more prominent for different meditators when they begin the subject of mentality, the Buddha himself taught:
paragraphs.M04-body-P058-S03:
Sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, abhiññeyyaṃ. — Bhikkhus, all is to be directly known. (Saṃyutta Nikāya, vol. 2, p. 258; Khuddaka Nikāya, vol. 9, p. 6.)
Sabbañca kho, bhikkhave, abhijānaṃ. — And, bhikkhus, when directly knowing all… (Saṃyutta Nikāya, vol. 2, p. 250.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P058-S04: He taught that one should endeavour to distinguish and know all conditioned phenomena called the truth of suffering and the truth of its origin by the three kinds of full understanding. To show that the meditator must distinguish with wisdom all actual phenomena suitable for discerning under the three characteristics, the commentator set out the foregoing method of apprehending mentality.
paragraphs.M04-body-P058-S05: The commentary’s instruction to apprehend the five with contact as fifth is a way of naming the principal phenomena. In the mental group of a single consciousness moment there are other mental phenomena besides those five. Since the other phenomena of the four mental aggregates are also present…

paragraphs.M04-body-P059-S01: … naming the five with contact as the fifth also comprises the four mental aggregates. That is why the commentary says to apprehend those five. They are named because they are common to all consciousnesses. Of the five, contact and volition belong to the formations aggregate. In that aggregate, volition is predominant. Therefore when instructed to apprehend contact and volition, one should apprehend those two principal phenomena together with the remaining associated phenomena belonging to the formations aggregate. Naming contact and volition embraces all the actual phenomena in the formations aggregate, because volition is predominant there. The Buddha himself also makes volition primary in analysing the formations aggregate in the sutta analysis of the Vibhaṅga (Abhidhamma, vol. 2, p. 37). This is an established principle. The remaining aggregates are named and taught directly. (Majjhima Nikāya Subcommentary, vol. 1, p. 370.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P059-S02: Under the guideline established in the texts, commentaries and subcommentaries, especially for a meditator wishing to apprehend sense-sphere mentality, after apprehending the subject of materiality, whether beginning with contact, feeling or knowing consciousness, apprehending mental phenomena within a consciousness moment is not a matter of taking only one contact, one feeling or one knowing consciousness…

paragraphs.M04-body-P060-S01: … then stubbornly holding to it like a frog clinging tightly, straining for minutes, hours, days, months or years, repeatedly apprehending and discerning that one phenomenon alone. All the phenomena associated with that contact, feeling or consciousness must also be apprehended and discerned. Good friends should put clear, upright wise attention first and receive and remember the instruction accordingly.
paragraphs.M04-body-P060-S03: It is difficult to use wisdom to break up the compactness that makes consciousness and mental factors arising according to the order of consciousness look like a solid mass, and to apprehend and discern them to the level of ultimate reality. Disciples nevertheless can apprehend and discern them. Some misunderstand the words of the Questions of King Milinda and thus say that disciples cannot discern those mental phenomena. To clear up the doubt, the explanations of the Saṃyutta Commentary and the Aṭṭhasālinī and the words of the Questions of King Milinda are given below.
paragraphs.M04-body-P060-S04:
Yathā hi tilatelaṃ sāsapatelaṃ madhukatelaṃ eraṇḍakatelaṃ vasātelanti imāni pañca telāni ekacāṭiyaṃ pakkhipitvā divasaṃ yamakamanthehi manthetvā tato “idaṃ tilatelaṃ, idaṃ sāsapatelan”ti ekekassa pāṭiyekkaṃ uddharaṇaṃ nāma dukkaraṃ, idaṃ tato dukkarataraṃ. Bhagavā pana sabbaññutaññāṇassa suppaṭividdhattā dhammissaro dhammarājā imesaṃ arūpīnaṃ dhammānaṃ ekārammaṇe vattamānānaṃ vavatthānaṃ…
Suppose five oils, sesame, mustard, madhuka, castor and animal fat, are poured together in one vessel and stirred all day. It is difficult to separate them and declare, “This is sesame oil, this is mustard oil.” Still more difficult is what the Blessed One, the All-knowing, Master and King of the Dhamma, accomplished in distinguishing immaterial phenomena operating on one object…

M04-body-P061.title: The similes of mixed oils and the waters of five rivers

paragraphs.M04-body-P061-S01:
… akāsi. Pañcannaṃ mahānadīnaṃ samuddaṃ paviṭṭhānaṃ “idaṃ gaṅgāya udakaṃ, idaṃ yamunāyā”ti evaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ udakuddharaṇenāpi ayamattho veditabbo.
… Understand this meaning also from the simile of the water in the ocean into which five great rivers flow. It is difficult to distinguish and say, “This is water from the Gaṅgā, this is water from the Yamunā,” and so on. (Saṃyutta Nikāya Commentary, vol. 2, p. 271.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P061-S02:
Imesañca pana phassapañcamakānaṃ dhammānaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ vinibbhogaṃ katvā paññattiuddharaṇena bhagavatā dukkaraṃ kataṃ. Nānāudakānañhi nānātelānaṃ vā ekabhājane pakkhipitvā divasaṃ nimadditānaṃ vaṇṇagandharasānaṃ nānatāya disvā vā ghāyitvā vā sāyitvā vā nānākaraṇaṃ sakkā bhaveyya ñātuṃ. Evaṃ santampi taṃ dukkaraṃ vuttaṃ. Sammāsambuddhena pana imesaṃ arūpīnaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ dhammānaṃ ekārammaṇe vattamānānaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ vinibbhogaṃ katvā paññattiuddharaṇena atidukkaraṃ kataṃ. Tenāha āyasmā Nāgasenatthero:
The Blessed One accomplished a difficult task when he analysed the five with contact as the fifth and named each separately. If waters and oils of different colours, odours and flavours are mixed together in one vessel and stirred throughout the day, their differences in colour, smell and taste can still be distinguished to some extent by looking, smelling or tasting. Thus the distinction of mental phenomena is called difficult. The Fully Awakened One did what is more difficult in analysing and naming each immaterial consciousness and mental factor operating on one object. Hence Venerable Nāgasena said:
paragraphs.M04-body-P061-S03:
Dukkaraṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā katanti. Kiṃ, bhante Nāgasena, bhagavatā dukkaraṃ katanti? Dukkaraṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā kataṃ, yaṃ imesaṃ arūpīnaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ dhammānaṃ ekārammaṇe pavattamānānaṃ vavatthānaṃ akkhātaṃ: “ayaṃ phasso, ayaṃ vedanā, ayaṃ saññā, ayaṃ cetanā, idaṃ cittan”ti. Opammaṃ, bhante, karohīti.
“Great king, the Blessed One did something difficult.”
“Venerable Nāgasena, what difficult thing did the Blessed One do?”
“Great king, the Blessed One did something difficult. He distinguished the immaterial consciousness and mental factors operating on one object: ‘This is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is volition, this is consciousness.’”
“Give me a simile, venerable sir.”
paragraphs.M04-body-P061-S04:
Yathā, mahārāja, kocideva puriso nāvāya samuddaṃ ajjhogāhetvā hatthapuṭena udakaṃ gahetvā jivhāya sāyitvā jāneyya nu kho, mahārāja, so puriso “idaṃ gaṅgāya udakaṃ, idaṃ yamunāya udakaṃ, idaṃ aciravatiyā udakaṃ, idaṃ sarabhuyā udakaṃ, idaṃ mahiyā udakan”ti? Dukkaraṃ, bhante, jānitunti.
“Great king, suppose a man went out into the ocean in a boat, scooped up water in his cupped hand, and tasted it with his tongue. Could he know, ‘This is water from the Gaṅgā, this from the Yamunā, this from the Aciravatī, this from the Sarabhū, this from the Mahī’?”
“It would be difficult to know, venerable sir.”

M04-body-P062.title: The meaning of the simile for distinguishing mentality

paragraphs.M04-body-P062-S01:
Tato dukkarataraṃ kho, mahārāja, bhagavatā kataṃ, yaṃ imesaṃ arūpīnaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ dhammānaṃ, pe, “idaṃ cittan”ti.
“Great king, the Blessed One did what is more difficult than that in distinguishing those immaterial consciousness and mental factors: pe, ‘this is consciousness’.” (Abhidhamma Commentary, vol. 1, pp. 186–187; Milindapañha, p. 94.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P062-S02: The meaning of the Pāli text and commentaries above is as follows. When distinguishing and apprehending mental phenomena with wisdom, or discerning and investigating them in insight, for every moment of process-free consciousness, namely rebirth-linking, life-continuum and death, and every moment of process consciousness arising in its fixed order, one must apprehend and discern the mental phenomena headed by the five with contact as the fifth. This has already been explained.
paragraphs.M04-body-P062-S03: Within each consciousness moment, the Buddha distinguished each of the five with contact as the fifth and set out their names as contact, feeling, perception, volition and consciousness. In distinguishing them in this way, he accomplished a difficult task. The following simile makes it clear.
paragraphs.M04-body-P062-S04: Suppose waters differing in colour, odour and taste are placed in one pot and stirred diligently all day. Or suppose oils and fats differing in flavour, such as ghee, sesame oil, mustard oil, peanut oil, chicken fat and pork fat, are put in one large pan and stirred diligently from morning to evening.

M04-body-P063.title: Material phenomena in mixed waters and oils

paragraphs.M04-body-P063-S01: Even when different waters or oils have been mixed in the same vessel and stirred all day, their colours, odours and flavours remain distinct. By looking with the eye, smelling with the nose or tasting with the tongue, one may still recognize something of the differences between them.
paragraphs.M04-body-P063-S02: Note. Material phenomena arise only as tiny particles called material clusters. Water and oil are collections of clusters in which the nature and power of the water element predominate. The material phenomena in one cluster and those in another are separated by the space element, so they do not merge or associate. One with the eye of wisdom that sees ultimate reality can analyse, know and apprehend colour, odour and flavour within each cluster. Because this can be apprehended with wisdom, someone with knowledge of ultimate reality, even if unable to use ordinary eye-, nose- or tongue-sensitivity to tell apart the colours, odours and flavours of waters or oils mixed in one vessel and stirred all day, may still use the eye, nose and tongue of wisdom to recognize those differences within the waters or oils…

M04-body-P064.title: The Buddha’s distinction of individual mental phenomena

paragraphs.M04-body-P064-S01: … this is the point of the explanation. Though such recognition may still be possible, Venerable Nāgasena says in the Questions of King Milinda that distinguishing mental phenomena is difficult. The Fully Awakened Buddha, endowed with six excellences, had penetrated with omniscient knowledge and was truly King of the Dhamma, master of the teaching. Thus, for each consciousness and mental factor in the groups of mentality arising together and taking one object, he distinguished each separately by his knowledge and taught by assigning names: “This is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is volition, this is consciousness.” In teaching the Dhamma by setting out these distinct names, the Buddha performed a very difficult task.
paragraphs.M04-body-P064-S02: The point. For example, in one mind-door moment of great wholesome impulsion of knowledge distinguishing mentality and materiality, or of insight knowledge apprehending and distinguishing materiality, there are thirty-four mental phenomena, consciousness and mental factors, when both knowledge and joy are present. They arise together, cease together, share the same material support, the heart-base, and take one and the same object, the materiality being discerned. Were there no Fully Awakened Buddha endowed with omniscience, the teaching that distinguishes each by name, such as “this nature is contact, this nature…

M04-body-P065.title: The dialogue between Nāgasena and King Milinda

paragraphs.M04-body-P065-S01: … is feeling”, so that disciples can use wisdom to distinguish and know them through names such as contact and feeling, could not arise by any worldly means in the past, present or succeeding aeons. To clarify that meaning for King Milinda, the renowned Venerable Nāgasena used the simile of waters from five great rivers flowing into the ocean and spoke as follows.
paragraphs.M04-body-P065-S02:
“King Milinda, the Buddha accomplished a very difficult task.”
“Venerable Nāgasena, what very difficult task did the Buddha accomplish?”
“King Milinda, consciousness and mental factors are mental phenomena that arise together and take one object. The Buddha distinguished them as follows:
paragraphs.M04-body-P065-S03:
1. The phenomenon that touches this object is contact.
2. The phenomenon that experiences the flavour of this object is feeling.
3. The phenomenon that marks this object is perception.
4. The phenomenon that leads the associated phenomena to this object is volition.
5. The phenomenon that apprehends, that is, knows this object, is consciousness.
paragraphs.M04-body-P065-S04: By setting out these names, he distinguished each mental phenomenon that exists ultimately…

paragraphs.M04-body-P066-S01:
… and taught them in this way. In distinguishing and teaching each phenomenon, he accomplished a very difficult task.
“Venerable sir, please give a simile.”
paragraphs.M04-body-P066-S02:
“King Milinda, suppose a man goes out to sea by boat, scoops up water with his cupped hand and tastes it with his tongue. Could he know: (1) This is water from the Gaṅgā, (2) this from the Yamunā, (3) this from the Aciravatī, (4) this from the Sarabhū, (5) this from the Mahī?”
“Venerable Nāgasena, it would be difficult to know.”
paragraphs.M04-body-P066-S03: “King Milinda, consciousness and mental factors are mental phenomena that arise together on one object. He taught: (1) What touches this object is contact. Pe. (5) What apprehends, that is, knows this object, is consciousness. By setting out these names he distinguished and taught each ultimately existing mental phenomenon. In distinguishing and teaching them in this way…

M04-body-P067.title: The difficult task accomplished by the Buddha

paragraphs.M04-body-P067-S01: … the Buddha accomplished a very difficult task.” (Milindapañha, p. 94.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P067-S02: The meaning of the text and commentary above is this. In a single moment, consciousness and mental factors, which are ultimate phenomena, arise together taking one object. It is very difficult to distinguish each with knowledge, give it a name and teach “this is contact, this is feeling,” and so on. That is the point of the quotation. Disciples can still discern the mental phenomena in a single moment of consciousness. Understand this carefully. A mistaken understanding can lead to mistaken practice, so take particular care when applying it.
paragraphs.M04-body-P067-S03: Notice again the passage from the Aṭṭhasālinī quoted above.
paragraphs.M04-body-P067-S04:
Sammāsambuddhena pana imesaṃ arūpīnaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ dhammānaṃ ekārammaṇe vattamānānaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ vinibbhogaṃ katvā paññattiuddharaṇena atidukkaraṃ kataṃ.
The Fully Awakened Buddha accomplished something exceedingly difficult by distinguishing individually these immaterial consciousnesses and mental factors operating on one object and assigning their names. (Abhidhamma Commentary, vol. 1, p. 186.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P067-S05: In each consciousness moment taking one object, the Fully Awakened Buddha distinguished with omniscient knowledge each mental phenomenon, consciousness or mental factor: “This is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is volition…

paragraphs.M04-body-P068-S01: … this is consciousness.” The explanation stresses the great difficulty of naming and teaching each phenomenon in that way. That is the point to remember.
paragraphs.M04-body-P068-S02: An established principle to follow carefully when apprehending mentality is to apprehend base and object together. Venerable Sāriputta followed this principle. Take his discernment of the mentality of first jhāna as an example. The Buddha described it as follows:
paragraphs.M04-body-P068-S03:
Tyāssa dhammā anupadavavatthitā honti. Tyāssa dhammā viditā uppajjanti, viditā upaṭṭhahanti, viditā abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. So evaṃ pajānāti: “Evaṃ kirame dhammā ahutvā sambhonti, hutvā paṭiventī”ti.
He distinguished the phenomena one by one in sequence. He knew them as they arose, as they were present and as they disappeared. He understood: “These phenomena, not having been, come to be. Having come to be, they vanish.” (Majjhima Nikāya, vol. 3, p. 75.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P068-S04: Venerable Sāriputta knew each mental phenomenon of first jhāna individually in sequence. The jhāna mentality was evident to his knowledge as it arose, was present and ceased. In other words, he knew clearly its arising, presence…

M04-body-P069.title: How Venerable Sāriputta discerned the mentality of jhāna

paragraphs.M04-body-P069-S01: … and cessation. He knew clearly: “These mental phenomena of jhāna were not previously present and have now arisen afresh. Having arisen, they always quickly cease.” (Majjhima Nikāya, vol. 3, p. 75.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P069-S02: From first jhāna through the base of nothingness, he discerned the jhāna mental phenomena individually in sequence, by insight into each successive phenomenon (anupadadhamma-vipassanā). For the base of neither perception nor non-perception he grouped the jhāna mentality and discerned it collectively (kalāpasammasana). (Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, vol. 4, p. 61.) When discerning each phenomenon, he knew its arising, presence and cessation clearly. The commentary explains why.
paragraphs.M04-body-P069-S03:
Vatthārammaṇānaṃ pariggahitattāya. Therena hi vatthu ceva ārammaṇañca pariggahitaṃ. Tenassa tesaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādaṃ āvajjentassa uppādo pākaṭo hoti, ṭhānaṃ āvajjentassa ṭhānaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, vayaṃ āvajjentassa vayo pākaṭo hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “viditā uppajjanti, viditā upaṭṭhahanti, viditā abbhatthaṃ gacchantī”ti.
Because base and object had been apprehended. The elder had apprehended both. When he adverted to the arising of those phenomena, their arising was evident. When he adverted to their presence, it was evident. When he adverted to their dissolution, it was evident. Hence they were said to be known as they arose, were present and disappeared. (Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, vol. 4, p. 60.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P069-S04: The subcommentary explains that the bases and objects had already been apprehended with knowledge, including the jhāna phenomena occurring on that object. Pe. These are the phenomena of the attainment process. (Majjhima Nikāya Subcommentary, vol. 3, p. 278.) Venerable Sāriputta was able to discern in this way because he had apprehended base and object together…

M04-body-P070.title: The base and object to apprehend first

paragraphs.M04-body-P070-S01: … Before apprehending each mental phenomenon in a jhāna process, Venerable Sāriputta had apprehended both the supporting base, including the life-continuum mind-door at which those phenomena arise, and the corresponding jhāna object, such as the counterpart sign of breathing or of a kasiṇa. Thus when he attended to the arising, presence or cessation of the mentality in the process, each phase became evident to his knowledge. That is why the Buddha said he knew it when it arose, was present and ceased. (Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, vol. 4, p. 60.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P070-S02: Note. In the instruction to apprehend base and object together, “base” refers to the six doors: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind.
paragraphs.M04-body-P070-S03: For good friends wishing to practise meditation on mentality, this principle is as precious as a priceless gem. Develop meditation on mentality. But if base and object are not apprehended together, such a meditator…

paragraphs.M04-body-P071-S01: … sits with their back turned to the Buddha’s teaching. They will likely use the number of a hundred thousand koṭis to challenge the practice of mentality taught by the Buddha.
paragraphs.M04-body-P071-S02: As explained above, a meditator wishing to apprehend the mentality headed by the five with contact as the fifth must first apprehend materiality, especially the material base and material object. After apprehending that mentality, one is instructed to return to materiality as follows.
paragraphs.M04-body-P071-S03:
So ime phassapañcamakā kiṃnissitāti upadhārento “vatthunissitā”ti pajānāti. Vatthu nāma karajakāyo, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “idañca me viññāṇaṃ ettha sitaṃ ettha paṭibaddhan”ti. So atthato bhūtānicceva upādārūpāni ca.
Considering what supports the five with contact as fifth, one knows that they depend on a base. The base is the material body (karajakāya), as in the statement, “This consciousness of mine depends on this and is bound to this.” In actual terms that body consists of the great elements and derived materiality. (Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, vol. 1, p. 281; Abhidhamma Commentary, vol. 2, pp. 252–253.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P071-S04: The subcommentary explains that to delimit mentality and materiality, materiality must be apprehended without omission. Thus it says “the base is the material body”. In presenting the material body as the support, it quotes, “This consciousness of mine depends on this and is bound to this.” (Mūlaṭīkā, vol. 2, p. 157.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P071-S05: The meditator who has apprehended the mentality headed by the five with contact as fifth should investigate with wisdom: “Dependent on what do these mental phenomena arise?”…

M04-body-P072.title: The material body as the support

paragraphs.M04-body-P072-S01: … On investigating, one knows clearly that they arise dependent on a material base. The base is the material body. Regarding this body the Buddha taught: “This consciousness of mine is dependent on this material body and bound to it.” (Dīgha Nikāya, vol. 1, p. 72; Majjhima Nikāya, vol. 2, p. 209.) In actual phenomena, the material body comprises the great elements and derived materiality. (Dīgha Nikāya Commentary, vol. 2, pp. 314–315; Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, vol. 1, p. 281; Abhidhamma Commentary, vol. 2, pp. 252–253.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P072-S02: “There is no person, being, life, self, deva or brahmā, only mentality and materiality.” To attain knowledge delimiting mentality and materiality in that way, one must apprehend materiality without omission. Thus the commentary says “the base is the material body”. Here it includes the great elements and derived materiality present at the same location or door as the bases, all fifty-four or forty-four kinds of materiality at the corresponding door. To show that all the great elements and derived materiality of the material body constitute the support, the subcommentary quotes the Sāmaññaphala Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya, vol. 1, p. 72) and the Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya, vol. 2, p. 209). (Mūlaṭīkā, vol. 2, p. 157.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P072-S03: These are some guidelines for meditators wishing to apprehend mentality. Other guidelines…

M04-body-P073.title: From the guidelines to the cognitive processes

paragraphs.M04-body-P073-S01: … will be explained as the occasion arises. In apprehending mental phenomena there are six processes, beginning with the eye-door process. As the mind-door process has fewer process consciousnesses, the method will first be presented starting with the mind-door process. The Visuddhimagga instructs the tranquillity-vehicle practitioner to begin with the mind-door process of absorption impulsion (vol. 2, p. 222). Therefore the apprehension of jhāna mentality in the attainment process is presented first.
paragraphs.M04-body-P073-S02: Note. Mental phenomena in eye-door and mind-door processes taking visible form are called the visible-object track. Likewise, those in ear-door and mind-door processes taking sound form the sound track, those in nose-door and mind-door processes taking odour the odour track, those in tongue-door and mind-door processes taking taste the taste track, and those in body-door and mind-door processes taking a tangible object the tangible track. Mental phenomena in a mind-door process taking a mind-object, or any member of that class, form the mind-object track.

M04-body-P074.title: Part 3. Jhāna attainment with the breathing counterpart sign

paragraphs.M04-body-P074-S02: If you have developed the ten kasiṇas and attained the eight attainments, continue apprehending their mental phenomena in accordance with the following table.

paragraphs.M04-body-P075-S02:
Applied thought, sustained thought and joy. The stilling of applied and sustained thought is the surmounting of those two. Because both have subsided, the second jhāna is without them. (Visuddhimagga, vol. 1, p. 151.)
In the preliminary stage the sense-sphere consciousnesses are accompanied by applied thought, sustained thought and joy… (Abhidhamma Commentary, vol. 2, p. 237.) According to these explanations…

M04-body-P076.title: Jhāna factors at access and absorption

paragraphs.M04-body-P076-S01: … applied thought, sustained thought and joy are still associated with the sense-sphere access impulsions, such as preparation and access. Only in the absorption consciousnesses of second jhāna onward are applied and sustained thought absent, according to the fourfold reckoning. In the case of fourth jhāna, joy is also absent from the sense-sphere access impulsions. The Visuddhimagga explains this as follows.
paragraphs.M04-body-P076-S02: Pleasant feeling cannot serve as repetition condition for neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Since fourth jhāna must arise with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, those consciousnesses are associated with equanimity. Because of association with equanimity, joy also falls away. (Visuddhimagga, vol. 1, p. 160.) “Those consciousnesses” refers to the absorption consciousnesses and their related moments in that process. (Mahāṭīkā, vol. 1, p. 189.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P076-S03: This is the distinction. Since pleasant feeling cannot condition equanimous feeling by repetition, the four or five sense-sphere access impulsions and the absorption impulsions in a fourth-jhāna process are accompanied by equanimity. As these impulsions in the fourth-jhāna process are accompanied by equanimity, joy is also absent. (Visuddhimagga, vol. 1, p. 160; Mahāṭīkā, vol. 1, p. 189.)
