paragraphs.M04-body-P138-S01: In the very-great-object process, one past life-continuum moment has elapsed. Eye-sensitivity arising simultaneously with that past life-continuum is called medium-lived (majjhimāyuka). In the first great-object process there are two past life-continuum moments. Eye-sensitivity arising with the first of them is called medium-lived. In the second great-object process there are three past life-continuum moments. The first to sixth slight-object processes have four, five, six, seven, eight, and nine respectively. Counting from the life-continuum, the eye-sensitivity arising with the first past life-continuum is called medium-lived.
paragraphs.M04-body-P138-S02: From rebirth-linking through the seventeenth consciousness counting back from death consciousness, kamma-born materiality, including eye-sensitivity, arises continuously at the arising, presence and dissolution submoments of each consciousness throughout life. Depending on the strength of kamma, many clusters of each kind may arise at each submoment, including many eye-decads. When eye-consciousness occurs, their eye-sensitivities may be arising, present, or dissolving. Eye-consciousness mentality arises dependent on the strongest medium-lived eye-sensitivity among them.
paragraphs.M04-body-P138-S03: Sensitivities described as short-lived, long-lived and medium-lived all last seventeen consciousness moments. The names indicate their duration relative to the five-door object of the five-door process…

M04-body-P139.title: Three groups of sensitivity and the base of mind consciousness

paragraphs.M04-body-P139-S01: … according to whether they cease with, before, or after the object. In a very-great-object eye-door process, eye-sensitivity arising at the arising submoment of the past life-continuum ceases with the visible object that impinges on it, so is called medium-lived. Thirty-seven eye-sensitivities arising in moments before that past life-continuum cease before the visible object and are called short-lived. Eleven arising from the presence submoment of that past life-continuum through subsequent moments are still present when the visible object ceases and are called long-lived. Understand the same for the other eye-door processes and for ear-door processes and the rest.
paragraphs.M04-body-P139-S02: The five sense consciousnesses depend on sensitivity materiality that arose earlier and is still present when they arise, by the prenascence dependence condition. Of the three types of sensitivity, the Abhidhamma subcommentary determines that the five sense consciousnesses depend on the medium-lived type. The view that they depend on sensitivity arising with five-door adverting or with arrest of the life-continuum is rejected (Vīthipāṭha, pp. 2–3).
paragraphs.M04-body-P139-S03: For mind consciousness in an existence with five aggregates, rebirth-linking consciousness depends on the heart-base that arises with it. All mind consciousness from the life-continuum onward, including five-door adverting, receiving, investigating, determining, impulsion and registration, as well as mind-door adverting, impulsion and registration in mind-door processes, depends on the heart-base arising with the immediately preceding consciousness. On emerging from cessation attainment…

paragraphs.M04-body-P140-S01: … non-returner fruition or arahant fruition depends on the heart-base that arose one consciousness moment earlier. Near death, life-continuum, adverting and similar mind consciousnesses depend on the heart-base arising with the seventeenth consciousness counting back from death consciousness (Visuddhimagga, vol. 2, p. 279). Remember the following cases.
paragraphs.M04-body-P140-S02:
Heart-base serving as support
Consciousness | Depends on heart-base arising with
1. Rebirth-linking | That same consciousness
2. First life-continuum | Rebirth-linking
3. Second life-continuum | First life-continuum
4. Five-door adverting | Arrest of the life-continuum
5. Receiving | Sense consciousness
6. Investigating | Receiving
7. Determining | Investigating
8. First impulsion | Determining… pe…
9. Seventh impulsion | Sixth impulsion
10. First registration | Seventh impulsion
11. Second registration | First registration
paragraphs.M04-body-P140-S03: Remember these respective dependencies. Understand the mind-door processes in the same way.

M04-body-P141.title: Operation of five-door and mind-door processes

paragraphs.M04-body-P141-S01: Usually, in five-door processes and mind-door processes with sense-sphere impulsion, impulsion occurs seven times and registration twice. Each other process consciousness occurs once. After five-door processes such as the eye-door process, many mind-door processes can occur interspersed with life-continuum. The first is called the following mind-door process (tadanuvattaka). From the second mind-door process onward, the succeeding processes are called bare mind-door processes. Some teachers call them all following mind-door processes. The tables here simply say “mind-door process”.
paragraphs.M04-body-P141-S02:
Pañcamajavanepi … pe … na hotīti idaṃ pañcaviññāṇavīthiyaṃ itthipurisoti rajjanādīnaṃ abhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tattha hi āvajjanavoṭṭhabbanānaṃ ayoniso āvajjanavoṭṭhabbanavasena iṭṭhe itthirūpādimhi lobho, aniṭṭhe ca paṭigho uppajjati. Manodvāre pana itthipurisoti rajjanādi hoti.
The statement “even at the fifth impulsion … pe … it does not occur” refers to the absence, in the five-sense process, of lust and related reactions towards an object recognized as “woman” or “man”. In that process, unwise adverting and determining can give rise to greed for a desirable object such as a woman’s visible form, or to aversion towards an undesirable object. It is at the mind-door that lust and related reactions occur towards an object recognized as “woman” or “man”. (Mūlaṭīkā, vol. 2, p. 188.)
paragraphs.M04-body-P141-S03:
Tatthāyaṃ pavattikkamo, pañcadvāre rūpādiārammaṇe āpāthagate niyamitādivasena kusalākusalajavane uppajjitvā bhavaṅgaṃ otiṇṇe manodvārikajavanaṃ taṃyevārammaṇaṃ katvā bhavaṅgaṃ otarati. Puna tasmiṃyeva dvāre itthipurisotiādinā vavatthapetvā javanaṃ uppajjitvā bhavaṅgaṃ otarati. Puna vāre pasādarajjanādivasena javanaṃ javati.
Anuṭīkā, vol. 1, p. 200.
paragraphs.M04-body-P141-S04: In that sequence, at the five doors, when a visible object or the like enters range, wholesome or unwholesome impulsion arises through determination and related conditions, and the mind then subsides into life-continuum. The next mind-door process takes the same object, runs and returns to life-continuum. A further mind-door process identifies the entity in terms such as “female” or “male”, runs and returns to life-continuum. On a further turn, impulsion runs through faith, lust and similar conditions (Anuṭīkā, vol. 1, p. 200).

M04-body-P142.title: The first processes from visible form to recognition of colour

paragraphs.M04-body-P142-S01:
Saññaṃ paṭhamavīthena, tītaṃ dutiyacetasā. Nāmaṃ tatiyavīthena, atthaṃ catutthacetasā.
Perception in the first process, the past object in the second consciousness, the name in the third process, and the meaning in the fourth consciousness.
paragraphs.M04-body-P142-S02: 1. When visible form comes before the eye-door and mind-door, an eye-door process with wholesome or unwholesome impulsion arises in accordance with prior determination, such as “I will give rise only to the wholesome”, or the reverse. The mental phenomena in the eye-door process know only the colour of visible form and have yet to recognize a man, woman, pot, or cloth. At this point object and door merely meet. Wise attention can lead to wholesome impulsion, and unwise attention to unwholesome impulsion. These impulsions still take only the colour of the visible object, based on prior determination and other conditions.
paragraphs.M04-body-P142-S03:
2. After the eye-door process comes a mind-door process called the following mind-door process. It can take only the past visible object taken by the eye-door process. Wholesome or unwholesome impulsion may arise as appropriate. Counting the eye-door process, this is the second process. Registration may or may not occur.
3. After the second process comes a third, called the third bare mind-door process. This process…

M04-body-P143.title: Recognizing colour, convention, and the entity

paragraphs.M04-body-P143-S01: … knows that same past visible form as brown, yellow, blue, and so on. The first two processes know colour only. At the third process one distinguishes the particular colours. This process differentiates the past visible object seen through the previous two processes. Registration may or may not arise. Wholesome or unwholesome impulsion may occur according to wise or unwise attention.
paragraphs.M04-body-P143-S02: 4. The fourth bare mind-door process relies on the visible object seen and distinguished through the first three processes to know conventional entities such as man, woman, pot, cloth, robe, gold and silver. With a concept as object, registration has no opportunity to arise. If it takes only ultimate reality and continues to know just the colour of the visible object, registration may occur. Wholesome or unwholesome impulsion again depends on the manner of attention.
paragraphs.M04-body-P143-S03: 5. In the fifth bare mind-door process the particular conceptual entity can be distinguished as a man, woman, pot, cloth, gold, or silver. With wise attention, faith may arise. With unwise attention, attachment and affection may arise. An able insight meditator may take only ultimate colour in this process, giving registration an opportunity to occur. If the object is solely a concept, there is no such opportunity.

paragraphs.M04-body-P144-S01: 1. Determination (niyamita): deciding firmly to apply the mind to the wholesome, thinking “I should do only what is wholesome.” Wholesome impulsion arises through the strength of the mind resolved to practise generosity, virtue, meditation and other good deeds.
paragraphs.M04-body-P144-S02:
2. Inclination (pariṇāmita): drawing the mind away from the unwholesome and inclining it only to good deeds. Wholesome impulsion arises through the strength of the mind so inclined.
3. Habitual practice (samudācāra): continually practising generosity, virtue, tranquillity and insight and training the mind to occur continuously in wholesome states. Wholesome impulsion arises through the strength of the mind habituated to the wholesome.
paragraphs.M04-body-P144-S03: 4. Wise attention (ābhoga): living in a suitable place where the Triple Gem flourishes and good people live, relying on good persons such as the Buddha, hearing the true Dhamma concerning the Four Noble Truths, and having previously made merit. Owing to these conditions one knows how to attend by the right means and on the right path. Wholesome impulsion arises through the strength of this wise attention. Through these conditions wholesome impulsion arises (Abhidhamma Commentary, vol. 1, p. 117).

M04-body-P145.title: Four wholesome conditions and discerning the visible-object group

paragraphs.M04-body-P145-S01: One who has resolved, “Whatever object I encounter, I will give rise only to wholesome consciousness,” has wholesome consciousness. One who guards the mind against the unwholesome and inclines it to the wholesome has wholesome consciousness. One already habituated to wholesome consciousness also commonly has wholesome consciousness. One able to attend in the right way in any undertaking, that is, with wise attention, also commonly has wholesome consciousness. Owing to these four conditions, even on encountering an attractive sign or desirable object, wholesome consciousness arises in place of greed.
paragraphs.M04-body-P145-S02: The wholesome visible-object group. Mentality taking visible form as object comprises eye-door and mind-door mentality. After one eye-door process, many mind-door processes can arise, with numerous life-continuum moments intervening. The commentary to the Meghiya Sutta says that in an extremely brief interval, such as a blink, flash of lightning or snap of the fingers, countless consciousnesses can arise and cease (Aṅguttara Commentary, vol. 2, p. 325). Many eye-door and mind-door processes can therefore occur in such a short time.
paragraphs.M04-body-P145-S03: Some of those processes can be discerned and others cannot yet be discerned. Use wisdom to analyse and break down the compactness of mentality, apprehending the processes that you can discern and catch until ultimate phenomena are seen…

M04-body-P146.title: Four process types according to the remaining duration of the object

paragraphs.M04-body-P146-S01: … The four kinds of compactness of mentality are explained on pp. 209–217 of this book. Depending on the object’s remaining lifespan when the meditator catches it, there are four cases.
paragraphs.M04-body-P146-S02:
1. Only life-continuum vibration occurs (moghavāra).
2. The process goes as far as determining (voṭṭhabbanavāra).
3. It reaches impulsion (javanavāra).
4. It reaches registration (tadārammaṇavāra).
paragraphs.M04-body-P146-S03: Of the four types, the sample tables use the registration process as the main example. Meditators can gradually understand the other processes as they discern. The Aṭṭhasālinī calls the first three the first, second and third abortive courses, since they respectively lack process consciousness, impulsion and registration (Abhidhamma Commentary, vol. 1, p. 130).
